title: Secret compacts against unjust laws
english: The first charge Celsus brings, in his wish to discredit Christianity, is that Christians make compacts with one another in secret, against what the laws have established. His ground is that some compacts are open, those made in keeping with the laws, while others are hidden, those carried out against what the laws have established. He also wants to discredit what is called the love of Christians for one another, as something that springs from their common danger and is stronger than any oath.

Since, then, he keeps harping on the common law, and says that the compacts of Christians are against it, we must answer as follows. Suppose a man found himself among the Scythians, whose laws are lawless, and, with no chance to get away, were forced to live among them. Such a man would have good reason, because of the law of truth, which in the eyes of the Scythians is lawlessness, to make compacts with those who think as he does, against what the Scythians have established. In the same way, when truth sits in judgment, the laws of the nations about images and their godless worship of many gods are laws of Scythians, or of anything still more impious than Scythians. It is therefore not unreasonable to make compacts against what is established, when they are made for the sake of truth.

For if men made secret compacts to put to death a tyrant who had seized control of the city, they would do well. So it is with Christians: since the one they call the devil, and falsehood with him, rule as tyrants, they make compacts against what the devil has established, compacts against the devil and for the salvation of others, whom they may be able to persuade to break away from that law, which is, as it were, the law of Scythians and of a tyrant.

title: A doctrine of barbarian origin
english: Next he says that the doctrine is barbarian in its origin, meaning, evidently, Judaism, on which Christianity depends. And he is fair enough not to reproach our teaching for having its beginning among barbarians; indeed he praises the barbarians as able to discover doctrines. But he adds that the Greeks are better at judging what the barbarians discovered, at confirming it, and at putting it into practice for the sake of virtue.

From his own words, then, we have this to say in defense of what Christianity holds, which is true: anyone who comes to our teaching from the doctrines and training of the Greeks would not only judge these things to be true, but, having put them into practice, would also prove them, and would supply whatever seems to be lacking by the standard of Greek demonstration, and so establish the truth of Christianity.

We must say further that our teaching has a demonstration of its own, more divine than the Greek demonstration drawn from dialectic. This more divine demonstration the apostle calls a demonstration “of the Spirit and of power” (1 Corinthians 2:4): “of the Spirit” because of the prophecies, which are able to bring the reader to faith, above all in what concerns Christ; and “of power” because of the wondrous works of power. That these took place must be shown from many other things, and also from this, that traces of them are still preserved among those who live according to the purpose of our teaching.

title: Danger, philosophy and persecution
english: After this he speaks of Christians doing and teaching in secret what pleases them, and says that they have good reason for doing so, since they are warding off the death penalty that hangs over them. He compares this danger with the dangers that befell men for the sake of philosophy, as with Socrates; he might also have said, as with Pythagoras and other philosophers.

To this we must reply that in the case of Socrates the Athenians repented at once, and no bitterness toward him remained among them, nor in the case of Pythagoras. The Pythagoreans, at any rate, kept up their schools for a long time in Italy, in the region called Great Greece. But in the case of the Christians, the Roman senate, the emperors of the day, the soldiery, the common people, and the relatives of believers made war on our teaching, and they would have stopped it, overcome by the plotting of so many, had it not risen above them and surmounted them by divine power, so as to conquer the whole world that plotted against it.

title: Moral teaching written on every heart
english: Let us see also how he thinks he can discredit our moral teaching on the ground that it is shared with the other philosophers, and so is no venerable or new lesson. To this we must say that for those who teach a just judgment of God, punishment for sins would have been ruled out if all men did not have, by the common notions, a sound preconception about moral matters. It is therefore no wonder that the same God has sown in the souls of all men what he taught through the prophets and the Savior, so that every man may be without excuse at the divine judgment, having the intent “of the law written” in his own heart (Romans 2:15).

Scripture hinted at this in what the Greeks consider a myth, where it represents God as having written the commandments with his own “finger” (Exodus 31:18) and given them to Moses; and the wickedness of those who made the calf “broke” them (Exodus 32:19), as if it were saying that the flood of sin swept them away. Then God wrote them a second time and gave them, after Moses had hewn the stones (Exodus 34:1), as though the prophetic word were preparing the soul, after the first sin, for a second writing from God.

title: Against gods made with hands
english: Setting out our views on idolatry as something peculiar to those who follow our teaching, he even supplies an argument for them, saying that for this reason they do not believe in gods made with hands: it is not reasonable that things made by the basest of craftsmen, men of wicked character, should be gods, when they have often been fashioned by unjust men as well.

Then, in what follows, wishing to make this a common view, on the ground that it was not first discovered by our teaching, he sets out a saying of Heraclitus: “Those who approach lifeless things as gods act like someone chatting with houses” (Heraclitus, fragment 5). So about this too we must say that, as with the rest of moral teaching, notions were sown in men, and from them Heraclitus, and any other Greek or barbarian, thought of arguing this point. For he also points out that the Persians hold this view, citing Herodotus, who reports it (Herodotus, Histories 1.131).

We too will add that Zeno of Citium also says in his Republic: “There will be no need to build temples; for no temple ought to be thought of great worth or holy, since it is the work of builders and mechanics.” It is clear, then, that with this doctrine too, what must be done has been written “in the hearts” of men (Romans 2:15) in God's own writing.

title: The name of Jesus, not spells
english: After this Celsus says (what moves him to it I do not know) that Christians appear to gain their power by the names of certain demons and by incantations. He is hinting, I suppose, at those who cast spells on demons and drive them out. But he seems plainly to be slandering our teaching. For Christians do not appear to gain their power by incantations, but by the name of Jesus, together with the telling of the stories about him. These words, when spoken, have often made demons depart from men, especially when those who say them speak from a sound disposition of genuine faith.

Indeed, the name of Jesus has such power against demons that it is sometimes effective even when named by bad men. Jesus taught this when he said: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘In your name we cast out demons and did mighty works’” (Matthew 7:22). Whether Celsus passed over this on purpose and with malice, or from ignorance, I do not know.

In what follows he also accuses the Savior, saying that it was by sorcery that he was able to do the marvels he appeared to have done; and that he foresaw that others too, having learned the same lessons, would do the same thing and would boast that they did it by the power of God; and that Jesus drives such men out of his own commonwealth. And he accuses him thus: if he drives them out justly, while he himself is liable to the same charges, he is a bad man; but if he is not a bad man for having done these things, neither are those who act as he did.

But to speak plainly: even if it seems impossible to put to the test how Jesus did these things, it is clear that Christians use no practice of spells, but the name of Jesus and other words believed in accordance with the divine Scripture.

title: A secret doctrine known to the whole world
english: Next, since he often calls our doctrine secret, we must refute him on this point too, for nearly the whole world knows the preaching of Christians better than the opinions of the philosophers. For who is unaware of Jesus' birth from a virgin, and of the Crucified, and of his resurrection, believed by many, and of the judgment that is proclaimed, which will punish sinners as they deserve and count the righteous worthy of reward? Even the mystery of the resurrection, though not understood, is widely talked about, and unbelievers laugh at it. In view of all this, to say that the doctrine is secret is quite absurd.

That there are some things, as it were, beyond the outward teachings, which do not reach the many, is not peculiar to the Christian teaching alone; it is true of the philosophers as well. Among them some discourses were outward and others inward. Some heard Pythagoras on the principle “He said it himself,” while others were taught in secret the things not fit to reach ears that were profane and not yet purified. And all the mysteries everywhere, throughout Greece and the barbarian world, are secret, yet they have not been discredited for it. So it is in vain that he discredits the secret element in Christianity, when he has not even understood it accurately.

title: Celsus the Epicurean contradicts himself
english: With some cleverness he seems in a way to speak up for those who bear witness to Christianity even to death, when he says: “And I do not say that a man who holds to a good doctrine ought, if he is going to be in danger among men because of it, to abandon the doctrine, or pretend that he has abandoned it, or deny it.” And he condemns those who hold the beliefs of Christianity but pretend not to hold them, or deny them, saying that one who holds the doctrine ought not to pretend that he has abandoned it, or deny it.

We must show, then, that Celsus contradicts himself. From other writings of his he is found to be an Epicurean. But here, so that his accusation of our teaching may seem more reasonable, he does not admit to the views of Epicurus. Instead he pretends that there is in man something better than the earthly, akin to God, and he says that in those in whom this is in good health (that is, the soul), “it reaches out in every way toward what is akin to it” (he means God), “and they long always to hear something about him and to be reminded of him.”

See, then, how counterfeit his soul is. Having said beforehand that a man who holds to a good doctrine, even if he is going to be in danger among men because of it, must not abandon the doctrine, nor pretend that he has abandoned it, nor deny it, he himself falls into every one of the opposite faults. For he knew that if he admitted he was an Epicurean, he would have no credibility in accusing those who, in whatever way, teach a providence and set God over all that exists. We have learned that there were two Epicureans named Celsus: the earlier under Nero, and this one under Hadrian and later.

title: Faith for those who cannot study
english: After this he urges people to accept doctrines by following reason and a rational guide, since anyone who assents to anything in another way is sure to be deceived. He likens those who believe without reason to the begging priests of the Great Mother and to readers of portents, to the devotees of Mithras and of Sabazius, and to whatever one happens to meet: the apparitions of Hecate, or of some other female spirit, or of spirits. For just as among these, wicked men often take advantage of the ignorance of the gullible and lead them wherever they wish, so, he says, it happens among the Christians too. He says that some, who are not even willing to give or to receive an account of what they believe, use the sayings “Do not examine, but believe” and “Your faith will save you” (Mark 5:34; Luke 7:50). And he says that they say: “Wisdom in the world is an evil thing, and foolishness a good one” (1 Corinthians 3:18–19).

To this we must reply that if it were possible for everyone to leave the business of life and devote themselves to philosophy, no one should follow any other way than this alone. For in Christianity there will be found, to say nothing more boastful, no less examination of what is believed, and explanation of the riddles in the prophets, of the parables in the Gospels, and of countless other things that happened or were laid down in the law as symbols. But if this is impossible, partly because of the necessities of life and partly because of human weakness, since very few press eagerly toward rational study, what better method of helping the many could be found than the one handed down to the nations by Jesus?

And we ask, concerning the multitude of believers who have put away the great flood of wickedness in which they once wallowed: is it better for them, believing without reason, to have had their ways somehow restrained, and to have been helped by their belief that people are punished for sins and honoured for good works? Or is it better to refuse their conversion on bare faith until they give themselves to the examination of arguments? For plainly all of them, apart from a very few, will not receive even what they have received from believing simply, but will remain in a most wicked life.

If, then, anything else serves to prove that the Word’s love for humankind has come into human life not without God, this too must be counted with those proofs. For a devout person will not suppose that even a physician of bodies, who has brought many of the sick to better health, visits cities and nations without God; for nothing good comes about among human beings without God. And if one who has healed the bodies of many, or brought them to better health, does not heal without God, how much more is this true of one who has healed, converted and bettered the souls of many, who has made them depend on God who is over all, and has taught them to refer every action to what pleases him and to shun everything displeasing to God, down to the least of the things said or done, or even entering the mind?

title: Philosophers also begin by believing
english: Next, since they keep harping on faith, we must say this. We accept faith as useful for the many, and we admit that we teach those who cannot leave everything and pursue the examination of reason to believe even without reason; they do not admit this, yet they do it in practice. For who, when he has been urged toward philosophy and has thrown himself, as if by lot, into some school of philosophers, or has come to it because he happened upon a particular teacher, comes to it for any other reason than that he believes that school to be better? For he does not wait to hear the arguments of all the philosophers and of the different schools, the refutation of some and the proof of others, and only then choose to be a Stoic, a Platonist, a Peripatetic, an Epicurean, or a member of any school of philosophers whatever. Rather, by some irrational impulse, even if they do not wish to admit it, they come to practise, say, the Stoic teaching, leaving the others aside; they look down on the Platonic as humbler than the rest, or on the Peripatetic as the most human of all, and as admitting human goods more candidly than the other schools.

And some, troubled at their first encounter with the question of providence by what happens on earth to the bad and to the good, have too hastily assented to the view that there is no providence at all, and have chosen the doctrine of Epicurus and Celsus.

title: All of life rests on trust
english: If, then, as our argument has shown, one must believe some one of those who founded schools among Greeks or barbarians, how much more must one believe the God who is over all, and the one who teaches that he alone must be worshipped, and that all else must be disregarded, either as not existing, or as existing and worthy of honour, yet not of adoration and worship? On these matters, the one who does not only believe but also contemplates things by reason will set out the proofs that occur to him and that he finds by diligent searching.

And since all human affairs depend on faith, how is it not more reasonable to believe God rather than those men? For who sails, or marries, or has children, or casts seed upon the ground, without believing that things will turn out for the better, though the opposite may happen and sometimes does? Yet the belief that things will turn out for the better and as one prays makes everyone venture even on what is uncertain and might fall out otherwise. And if hope, and the more hopeful belief about the future, holds life together in every action whose outcome is uncertain, how much more reasonably will this faith be embraced by one who trusts, more than in the sea that is sailed, the earth that is sown, the wife who is married and the other affairs of human life, in the God who made all these things? And how much more in him who, with surpassing greatness of mind and divine magnanimity, dared to set this teaching before people in every part of the world, amid great dangers and a death thought shameful, all of which he endured for humankind; and who taught also those first persuaded to serve his teaching to dare, amid every danger and the deaths they always expected, to go abroad into every part of the world for the salvation of human beings?

title: Celsus’s claim to know everything
english: Then Celsus says, in these very words: “If they are willing to answer me, not as one who is testing them (for I know everything), but as one who cares for all alike, it would be well. But if they will not, and say, as they usually do, ‘Do not examine,’ and so on, then they must,” he says, “explain both what kind of things these are that they speak of, and from what source they have flowed,” and so on.

To his “for I know everything,” a most boastful thing for him to have ventured, we must reply this. If he had read above all the prophets, which are admittedly full of riddles and of words obscure to the many; if he had read the Gospel parables, the rest of the writing of the law and of Jewish history, and the sayings of the apostles; and if, having read them, he had been willing in good faith to enter into the meaning of the words, he would not have been so bold, nor said, “for I know everything.” Even we, who have spent long study on these writings, would not say “I know everything,” for we love the truth. None of us will say, “I know all of Epicurus,” or will dare to claim that he knows all of Plato, when there are so many disagreements even among those who expound them. For who is so bold as to say, “I know all the Stoic teaching,” or “all the Peripatetic”? Unless perhaps his “I know everything” comes from this: he heard from some ignorant and senseless people, who are unaware of their own lack of learning, and supposed that, having had such teachers, he had come to know everything.

He seems to me to have done something like this. Suppose someone visited Egypt, where the wise men of the Egyptians, following their ancestral writings, pursue much philosophy about what they hold to be divine, while the common people hear certain myths whose meaning they do not understand and pride themselves greatly on them; and suppose he thought he knew everything Egyptian, after becoming a pupil of their common people, without mixing with any of the priests or learning the secret teachings of the Egyptians from any of them. What I have said about the wise and the common people of the Egyptians can also be seen among the Persians. They have rites which their learned men honour with understanding, but which the many and more superficial among them perform symbolically. The same must be said of the Syrians and the Indians, and of all who have both myths and writings.

title: Foolishness to this age
english: Celsus has set down, as something said by many Christians, “Wisdom in this life is an evil thing, and foolishness a good one.” We must reply that he slanders our teaching, for he did not set out the actual words found in Paul, which run thus: “If anyone among you thinks he is wise, let him become foolish in this age, so that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Corinthians 3:18–19). So the apostle does not say simply, “Wisdom is foolishness with God,” but “the wisdom of this world”; and again he does not say without qualification, “If anyone among you thinks he is wise, let him become foolish,” but “let him become foolish in this age, so that he may become wise.” By “the wisdom of this age,” then, we mean every philosophy that holds false opinions, which according to the Scriptures is being brought to nothing (1 Corinthians 2:6); and we call foolishness good not absolutely, but when someone becomes “foolish” to this age.

It is as if we were to say that the Platonist too, who believes in the immortality of the soul and in what is said of it concerning its passing into other bodies, has taken up foolishness in the eyes of the Stoics, who mock assent to these things; in the eyes of the Peripatetics, who keep talking of Plato’s “twitterings” (Aristotle, Posterior Analytics 1.22, 83a33); and in the eyes of the Epicureans, who charge with superstition those who bring in providence and set God over the universe.

Further, that even in the judgement of the Word it is far better to assent to doctrines with reason and wisdom than with bare faith, and that the Word willed this also because circumstances required it, so as not to leave human beings wholly without help, is shown by Paul, the true disciple of Jesus, when he says: “For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of the preaching to save those who believe” (1 Corinthians 1:21). These words clearly show that God ought to have been known in the wisdom of God; and since this did not happen so, God was pleased, as a second course, to save those who believe, not through foolishness without qualification, but through foolishness so far as the preaching goes. For Jesus Christ crucified, when he is preached, is at first sight the foolishness of the preaching; as Paul too, who was aware of this, says in the passage: “But we preach Jesus Christ crucified, to Jews a stumbling block and to Gentiles foolishness, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:23–24).

title: Why single out the Jews?
english: Celsus thinks that many nations share a kinship in this same doctrine, and he names all these nations as having originated such a teaching. Yet I do not know how it is that he slanders the Jews alone, not counting their nation with the rest, as one that either shared their studies and was of one mind with them, or taught much the same on many points. It is fair, then, to ask him why he has believed the histories of barbarians and Greeks about the antiquity of the nations he named, while he makes out the histories of this one nation alone to be false. For if each people set down its own affairs out of love for the truth, why should we distrust the prophets of the Jews alone? But if Moses and the prophets wrote many things about their own affairs to favour their own cause, why shall we not say the same about the writers of the other nations too? Or are the Egyptians to be trusted about the Jews when they speak ill of them in their histories, while the Jews are lying when they say the same things about the Egyptians, recording that they themselves suffered much unjustly and saying that for this reason the Egyptians were punished by God?

Nor is this to be said of the Egyptians alone. For we shall find conflict between the Assyrians and the Jews, and this is recorded in the ancient histories of the Assyrians. In the same way the Jewish writers (so as not to seem to beg the question by saying “the prophets”) recorded that the Assyrians were their enemies. See at once, then, the partiality of a man who believes some nations as wise and condemns others as utterly foolish. For listen to Celsus saying: “There is an ancient doctrine that goes back to the beginning, with which the wisest nations and cities and wise men have always been occupied.” Yet he would not call the Jews one of the wisest nations, not even on a level with the Egyptians, Assyrians, Indians, Persians, Odrysians, Samothracians and Eleusinians.

title: Pagan witnesses to Jewish wisdom
english: How much better than Celsus is Numenius the Pythagorean! He showed in many works that he was a man of the greatest learning, he tested more doctrines, and he gathered from more sources what seemed to him to be true. In the first book of his work On the Good, speaking of the nations that have conceived of God as incorporeal, he placed the Jews among them as well, and in his treatise he did not hesitate to use even the words of the prophets and to interpret them figuratively.

It is also said that Hermippus, in the first book of his work On Lawgivers, recorded that Pythagoras brought his own philosophy from the Jews to the Greeks. And a book about the Jews is current under the name of Hecataeus the historian, in which he takes the nation’s part as a wise one so markedly that Herennius Philo, in his treatise on the Jews, first doubts whether the treatise is really the historian’s, and then says that, if it is his, he was probably carried away by the persuasiveness he found among the Jews and assented to their teaching.

title: Moses struck from the list of the wise
english: I am surprised that Celsus places the Odrysians, the Samothracians, the Eleusinians and the Hyperboreans among the most ancient and wisest nations, yet has not seen fit to admit the Jews either among the wise or among the ancient, although many writings are current among Egyptians, Phoenicians and Greeks that bear witness to their antiquity. I thought it needless to set these out, for anyone who wishes can read what Flavius Josephus wrote in his two books on the antiquity of the Jews, where he brings together a large collection of writers who bear witness to the antiquity of the Jews. There is also the Address to the Greeks by Tatian, a later writer, who sets out with great learning those who have written about the antiquity of the Jews and of Moses. It seems, then, that Celsus says these things not truthfully but out of hostility, his aim being to bring a charge against the origin of Christianity, which depends on the Jews.

What is more, he says that Homer’s Milk-drinkers (Homer, Iliad 13.5–6), the Druids of the Gauls and the Getae are very wise and ancient nations, holding views akin to the Jewish doctrines; whether any writings of theirs are extant I do not know. But the Hebrews alone, so far as it lies with him, he shuts out from both antiquity and wisdom. Again, when he draws up a list of ancient and wise men who helped the people of their own time, and through their writings those who came after, he shut Moses out of the list of the wise. Yet of Linus, whom Celsus put first among those he named, no laws or discourses are extant that have turned nations around and healed them; whereas a whole nation, scattered over the whole inhabited world, carries the laws of Moses.

See, then, whether it was not out of open malice that he shut Moses too out of the list of the wise, while saying that Linus, Musaeus, Orpheus, Pherecydes, Zoroaster the Persian and Pythagoras held views on these matters, that their doctrines were set down in books, and that they have been preserved to this day. And he chose to forget the myth about the so-called gods as subject to human passions, which Orpheus above all wrote down.

title: Allegory allowed for the gods but not for Moses
english: In what follows, while accusing the history written by Moses, he finds fault with those who interpret it figuratively and allegorically. One might say to this most noble man, who gave his own book the title True Doctrine: “Why on earth, sir, do you speak with reverence of the records that gods fell into such great calamities as your wise poets and philosophers describe, that they engaged in abominable unions, made war on their fathers and castrated them, and that they dared, did and suffered such things? And yet when Moses says nothing of the kind about God, nor even about holy angels, but tells far lesser things about men (for no one in his writings dared what Cronus did against Uranus, nor what Zeus did against his father, nor did ‘the father of men and gods’ (Homer, Iliad 1.544) lie with his own daughter), do you people think that he leads astray those who received laws from him, and that they have been deceived?”

It seems to me that Celsus is doing something like Plato’s Thrasymachus, who would not allow Socrates to answer as he wished about justice, but said: “See that you do not say that the just is the advantageous, or what is needful, or anything else of that sort” (Plato, Republic 336c–d). For Celsus too, having accused (as he supposes) the histories in Moses, and having blamed those who allegorize them while also giving them some praise, saying they are “the more reasonable,” as it were prevents those who are able from making a defence that answers to the true nature of the matters, once he has made his accusations as he pleases.

title: Compare the books themselves
english: We would say, challenging him to set book beside book: “Bring out, sir, the poems of Linus, Musaeus and Orpheus and the writing of Pherecydes, and examine them together with the laws of Moses, setting histories beside histories, and moral discourses beside laws and commandments. See which are better able to turn those who hear them, even at the first hearing, and which of them might even ruin the listener. Observe how the company of your writers cared little for those who would read them in the plain sense, and wrote their own philosophy, as you say, only for those able to interpret it figuratively and allegorically. Moses, on the other hand, in his five books has acted like a noble orator who studies the figures of speech and everywhere puts forward the double sense of his wording with care: he neither gave the mass of the Jews under his law occasions of harm in matters of conduct, nor set before the few who are able to read with greater understanding, those who can search out his intent, a writing lacking in contemplation.

“And it seems that the books of your wise poets are not even preserved any longer, though they would have been kept if the reader had perceived any benefit. But the writings of Moses have moved many, even of those foreign to the Jewish way of life, to believe that, as the writings themselves declare, the One who first gave them as law and delivered them to Moses was God, who created the world. For it was fitting that the Maker of the whole world, who had laid down laws for the whole world, should give his words a power able to prevail over people everywhere. And I say this not yet examining the case of Jesus, but still showing that Moses, who is far less than the Lord, far surpasses, as the argument will establish, your wise poets and philosophers.”

title: Floods, fires, and the age of the world
english: Next, Celsus, wishing covertly to discredit the account of the making of the world given by Moses, which indicates that the world is not yet ten thousand years old but much less than that, sides with those who say that the world is uncreated, while hiding his own intention. For his statement that “there have been many conflagrations from all eternity, and many floods, and the flood in the time of Deucalion is more recent, having happened lately” plainly shows those able to understand him that in his view the world is uncreated.

Let the man who finds fault with the faith of Christians tell us by what demonstrative arguments he was compelled to accept that there have been many conflagrations and many floods, and that the most recent of all are the flood in the time of Deucalion and the conflagration in the time of Phaethon. But if he puts forward Plato’s dialogues on these matters, we shall tell him that we too may believe that the divine Spirit dwelt in the pure and devout soul of Moses, who rose above everything that has come into being and attached himself to the Creator of the universe, and who set forth the things of God far more clearly than Plato and the wise among Greeks and barbarians. And if he demands of us reasons for such a faith, let him first give reasons for what he himself declared without proof, and after that we shall establish that our own positions are so.

title: Egyptian riddles and Mosaic myths
english: Yet Celsus, even against his will, fell into bearing witness that the world is rather young and not yet ten thousand years old, when he said that the Greeks too consider these things ancient because, owing to the floods and conflagrations, they have neither seen nor remember anything older. Let the Egyptians, whom he counts the wisest, be Celsus’s teachers of the myth of conflagrations and inundations. The traces of their wisdom are irrational animals that are worshipped, and arguments to show that such worship of God is reasonable, and of a hidden and mystical kind.

If the Egyptians, to give dignity to their doctrine about the animals, offer theological explanations, they are wise. But if one who has assented to the law and the lawgiver of the Jews refers everything to the Creator of the universe, the only God, he is counted by Celsus and those like him inferior to one who brings divinity down not only into rational and mortal living beings but even into irrational ones. This goes beyond the mythical doctrine of transmigration, which tells of the soul falling from the vaults of heaven and descending as far as irrational animals, not only tame ones but even the most savage. And if the Egyptians tell myths, they are believed to have philosophized through riddles and secrets; but if Moses, writing for a whole nation, leaves them histories and laws, his words are thought to be empty myths that do not even admit of allegory.

title: If Moses learned it, what was his fault?
english: For this is what Celsus and the Epicureans think. “Moses, then,” he says, “having heard of this doctrine, which was current among wise nations and men of renown, won a godlike reputation.” To this we must reply, even granting him that Moses heard an older doctrine and handed it on to the Hebrews: if he heard a false doctrine, one neither wise nor venerable, and accepted it and handed it on to those under him, he is open to blame; but if, as you say, he assented to wise and true doctrines and educated his own people by means of them, what has he done that deserves accusation?

Would that Epicurus too had heard this doctrine, and Aristotle, who is less impious than he toward providence, and the Stoics, who said that God is a body! Then the world would not have been filled with teaching that sets providence aside, or curtails it, or brings in a corruptible first principle, the bodily one, according to which God too is a body for the Stoics. They are not ashamed to say that he is changeable, alterable through and through, and mutable, and in short capable of perishing if he had anything to destroy him, but fortunate enough not to perish because there is nothing to destroy him. Yet the doctrine of Jews and Christians, which preserves the unchangeableness and unalterableness of God, has been thought impious, because it does not join in impiety with those who hold impious views about God, saying in its prayers to the Divine, “But you are the same” (Psalm 102:27); and it is believed that God also said, “I do not change” (Malachi 3:6).

title: Circumcision and the name of Abraham
english: After this Celsus, without finding fault with the Jewish practice of circumcising the private parts, says that it "came from the Egyptians". In this he believes the Egyptians rather than Moses, who says that Abraham was the first among men to be circumcised (Genesis 17:24). Nor is Moses the only one to record the name of Abraham and to claim him as close to God. Many of those who charm demons with incantations also use the words "the God of Abraham" (Exodus 3:6) in their formulas. They achieve their effects through the name and through God's intimacy with that righteous man, and that is why they take up the phrase "the God of Abraham". Yet they do not know who Abraham is. The same must be said of Isaac, of Jacob and of Israel. These names, which everyone admits are Hebrew, are scattered in many places through Egyptian lore that claims to work some power.

As for the meaning of circumcision, which began with Abraham and was stopped by Jesus, who did not wish his disciples to do the same, it is not our purpose to explain it now. The present occasion is not for teaching about these matters but for a contest, to demolish the charges that Celsus brings against the doctrine of the Jews. He thinks he will more quickly prove Christianity false if, since its origin lies in the Jewish writings, he can by his accusations show that doctrine also to be false.

title: One world, one Maker
english: Next Celsus says that "the goatherds and shepherds who followed Moses as their leader were beguiled by rustic deceits and came to think there is one God." Since, as he thinks, goatherds and shepherds turned away from the worship of gods without reason, let him show, then, how he himself can establish the multitude of gods held by the Greeks, or by the other barbarian peoples. Let him show the real existence and substance of Mnemosyne bearing the Muses by Zeus, or of Themis bearing the Hours; or let him prove that the Graces, who are always naked, can truly exist in substance. But he will not be able to show from the facts that the inventions of the Greeks, which seem to be given bodily form, are gods. Why are the Greeks' myths about gods any truer than, say, those of the Egyptians? In their own language the Egyptians know nothing of Mnemosyne as mother of the nine Muses, nor of Themis as mother of the Hours, nor of Eurynome as one of the Graces, nor any of their other names.

How much more effective, then, and how much better than all these inventions it is to be persuaded by what we see, by the good order of the world, to worship its Maker as one, since the world is one and wholly in harmony with itself! For that reason it cannot have been made by many makers, just as it cannot be held together by many souls moving the whole heaven. For one soul is enough, which carries the whole sphere of the fixed stars from east to west and embraces within it all the things the world needs, things that are not complete in themselves. For all these are parts of the world, but God is no part of a whole, since God cannot be incomplete, as a part is incomplete. Yet perhaps a deeper account will show that God, in the proper sense, is not a whole either, just as he is not a part, since a whole is made up of parts. And reason does not allow us to accept that the God over all is made up of parts, each of which cannot do what the other parts do.

title: The names of God and the nature of names
english: After this he says that "the goatherds and shepherds thought there was one God, whether Most High, or Adonai, or the Heavenly One, or Sabaoth, or however and in whatever way they like to name this world; and they knew nothing more." And next he says that "it makes no difference whether one calls the God over all by the name current among the Greeks, Zeus, or by such-and-such a name, say, among the Indians, or by such-and-such among the Egyptians."

To this too we must reply that the present subject involves a deep and secret question: the question of the nature of names. Are names a matter of convention, as Aristotle thinks (Aristotle, On Interpretation 2)? Or are they by nature, as the Stoics hold, the first sounds imitating the things the names stand for, which is why the Stoics also bring in certain elements of etymology? Or are names by nature, as Epicurus teaches, though in a different way from what the Stoics think, because the first men burst out with certain sounds in response to things (Epicurus, Letter to Herodotus 75–76)?

Suppose, then, that in a treatment devoted to the subject we can establish the nature of names that have power, some of which are used by the wise among the Egyptians, or the learned among the Persian magi, or, among the philosophers of India, by the Brahmans or the Samanaeans, and so on in each of the nations. And suppose we can also prove that what is called magic is not, as the followers of Epicurus and Aristotle think, a thing wholly without coherence, but, as those skilled in it demonstrate, a coherent system, though its principles are known to very few. Then we shall say that the name Sabaoth, and Adonai, and the other names handed down among the Hebrews with great reverence, are not applied to ordinary, created things, but belong to a certain secret theology which refers to the Maker of the universe. This is why these names, when they are spoken with a certain sequence that is woven into them, can be employed for certain purposes; and so can others, current in the Egyptian tongue and applied to certain demons who can do only these particular things, and others, in the Persian language, applied to other powers; and so in each of the nations. And so it will be found that the names of the demons on earth, who have been allotted different places, are spoken in a way suited to the language of each place and nation.

Whoever, then, has with a nobler mind gained even a little insight into these matters will take care not to fit names to things that are not theirs. Otherwise he may suffer the same as those who wrongly apply the name "God" to lifeless matter, or who drag down the title "good" from the First Cause, or from virtue and the beautiful, to blind wealth, to the right proportion of flesh, blood and bones in health and good condition, or to what is counted noble birth.

title: Why Christians will not call God Zeus
english: And perhaps the danger is no less for one who brings the name of God, or the name of the good, down to things it should not be given to, than for one who interchanges the names that belong to a secret teaching, applying those of lesser things to greater, and those of greater things to lesser. I pass over the fact that with the name Zeus one at once hears along with it the son of Cronus and Rhea, the husband of Hera, the brother of Poseidon, the father of Athena and Artemis, and the one who lay with his daughter Persephone; or that with Apollo one hears the son of Leto and Zeus, the brother of Artemis, and the brother of Hermes on his father's side; and whatever else is told by those wise fathers of Celsus's doctrines, the ancient theologians of the Greeks. For what arbitrary choice lets the name Zeus be taken in its proper sense, but not also the statement that his father is Cronus and his mother Rhea? The same must be done with the other gods who are named.

But this charge in no way touches those who, according to a certain secret teaching, apply Sabaoth, or Adonai, or any of the other names to God. Whoever can philosophise about names in their hidden meanings would also find much about the names by which the angels of God are called: one of them is called Michael (Daniel 10:13), another Gabriel (Luke 1:19), and another Raphael (Tobit 12:15), names that fit the tasks they perform in the universe by the will of the God of all. Our Jesus too belongs to a like philosophy of names: his name has already been plainly seen to drive countless demons out of souls and bodies, taking effect upon those from whom they were driven out.

Further, on the topic of names it must be said that those skilled in the use of incantations report that the same incantation, spoken in its own language, can accomplish what the incantation promises; but translated into any other tongue whatever, it can be seen to be feeble and powerless. So it is not the meanings that stand for things, but the qualities and peculiarities of the sounds, that have a certain power in themselves for this purpose or that.

By such arguments we shall also defend the Christians for struggling even to death so as not to proclaim Zeus as God, nor to name him in another language. For they confess either the common name "God" without further definition, or with the addition, "the Maker of all, the Creator of heaven and earth (Psalm 146:6), who sent down to the human race these particular wise men"; for the name "God", joined to this designation, works a certain power among men. Much else could be said on the topic of names against those who think one need not care how they are used. And if Plato is admired for saying in the Philebus, "My fear, Protarchus, about the names of the gods is no small one" (Plato, Philebus 12c), because Philebus, who was conversing with Socrates, had called pleasure a goddess, how shall we not rather approve the reverent caution of the Christians, who attach to the Maker of the universe none of the names taken up in the mythologies? But enough of this for the present.

title: Not without God: the lives Jesus changed
english: Let us see how Celsus, who professes to know everything, slanders the Jews when he says that they "worship angels and are given to sorcery, in which Moses was their instructor." Where in the writings of Moses did he find the lawgiver handing down the worship of angels? Let him say, since he professes to know the teachings of Christians and Jews. And how is there sorcery among those who have accepted the law of Moses, and who have also read, "You shall not attach yourselves to enchanters, to be defiled by them" (Leviticus 19:31)? He promises to teach next how the Jews too went astray through ignorance and were deceived. Had he found ignorance among the Jews about Jesus the Christ, in that they did not heed the prophecies about him, he would truly have taught how the Jews went astray. As it is, without even caring to imagine these things, he takes for errors of the Jews what are not errors.

Celsus promises to teach about the Jews later, but first he makes his argument about our Saviour, as the one who led the way in our coming to be Christians. He says that "he became the leader of this teaching a very few years ago, and was thought by Christians to be the Son of God." On this very point, that he came a few years ago, we shall say this. Is it without God that Jesus, wishing in so few years to sow his word and teaching, has been able to do so much that in many parts of our inhabited world not a few Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish, have become so devoted to his word that they struggle even to death for Christianity rather than forswear him, which no one is recorded to have done for any other doctrine?

For my part, not flattering our teaching but trying to examine the facts with careful thought, I would say that not even those who heal many sick bodies reach the goal of bodily health without God. And if someone could free souls from the dissipation of vice, from licentious and unjust deeds, and from contempt for the divine, and could give as proof of such work a hundred people made better (let the argument be about that many), would not anyone reasonably say of him too that it was not without God that he had implanted in those hundred a word able to free them from so many evils? And if one who weighs these things fairly will grant that nothing better has come about among men without God, how much more confidently will he declare as much of Jesus, when he compares the former lives of many who come to his word with their later lives, and considers in how much licentiousness, how much injustice and greed each of them lived before they were "deceived", as Celsus and those who share his views say, and accepted a teaching which, as those men say, ruins human life; and how, from the time they received the word, they have become gentler, more dignified and steadier, so that some of them, for love of surpassing purity and for the sake of worshipping the divine more purely, do not even touch the sexual relations that the law permits.

title: A word that could not be stopped
english: Anyone who examines the facts will see that Jesus dared things beyond human nature, and that, having dared them, he accomplished them. From the beginning everyone worked against the sowing of his word through the whole world: the emperors of each age, the commanders-in-chief and governors under them, and, one might say, all who had been entrusted with any power whatever, as well as the magistrates of the cities, the soldiers and the common people. Yet his word prevailed, for as the word of God it is not of a nature to be hindered. Having proved stronger than so many opponents, it won the mastery over all Greece and, more widely still, over the barbarian world, and it turned countless souls to the worship of God that it teaches.

Since the unlearned and the rustic far outnumber those trained in learning, it was inevitable that, in a multitude won over by the word, the unlearned and rustic would far outnumber the more intelligent. But Celsus would not consider this. He thinks that the word’s love for humankind, which reaches every soul “from the rising of the sun” (compare Malachi 1:11; Psalm 113:3), is an unlearned thing, and that because it is unlearned and has no power at all in argument, it has won over only the unlearned. And yet even he does not say that the word has brought only the unlearned to the worship of God taught by Jesus; for he admits that among them there are some who are moderate, fair-minded and intelligent, and ready to read things as allegory.

title: Celsus’s Jew and the slander about Jesus’ birth
english: Celsus also makes use of an imagined speaker, imitating, in a way, a boy just starting at a rhetorician’s school, and he brings in a Jew who addresses Jesus with childish talk, nothing worthy of a philosopher’s grey hairs. Come, then, let us examine this too as best we can, and show that in what he says he has not even kept consistently to the character that suits a Jew.

After this he introduces a Jew conversing with Jesus himself and, as he thinks, refuting him on many points, but first on the charge that he made up his birth from a virgin. He also reproaches him with having been born in a Jewish village, of a local woman who was poor and worked with her hands for a living. He says that she was driven out by the man who had married her, a carpenter by trade, after she was convicted of adultery. Then he says that, cast off by her husband and wandering about in disgrace, she gave birth to Jesus in secret; and that Jesus, because he was poor, hired himself out as a labourer in Egypt, and there tried his hand at certain powers on which the Egyptians pride themselves; that he came back proud of these powers, and on account of them proclaimed himself God.

But to me, who cannot leave unexamined anything the unbelievers say, but who look into the origin of the facts, all these things seem to agree with Jesus’ having proved worthy of the prophecy that he is the Son of God.

title: Fame without rank, wealth or country
english: Among human beings, what helps a man become distinguished and famous, with his name spoken of everywhere, is birth, when his parents happen to be eminent and of high standing; the wealth of those who raised him and could afford to spend on their son’s education; and a fatherland that is great and renowned. But when someone who has everything opposite to these is able to rise above all that keeps him from becoming known, to stir those who hear of him, and to become conspicuous and well known to the whole world, a world that says conflicting things about him, how can we not marvel at such a nature, so plainly great in its gifts, setting its hand to great tasks, and possessing a boldness not to be lightly dismissed?

If one looked further into such a man’s life, how could one fail to ask how he, brought up in humble circumstances and poverty, having received no general education and having learned none of the arguments and doctrines that might have made him persuasive in addressing crowds, swaying the people and drawing more hearers, gave himself to teaching new doctrines? He brought the human race a teaching that set aside the customs of the Jews while still honouring their prophets, and that overthrew the laws of the Greeks, above all those concerning the divine. And how could such a man, brought up in this way, who had learned nothing of worth from any human being (as even those who speak evil of him admit), say such things about the judgment of God, about punishments for wickedness and honours for goodness, and say them in a way not easily despised, so that not only rustic and unlearned people were won by what he said, but also not a few of the more intelligent, those able to see into the hidden sense of sayings thought to be told in plain and humble words, a hidden sense that holds within it, so to speak, something more secret?

The man of Seriphus in Plato reproached Themistocles, who had become famous for his generalship, saying that he had won his fame not by his own character but by the good fortune of having the most celebrated fatherland in all Greece. He heard this reply from Themistocles, who was fair-minded and saw that his fatherland too had contributed to his fame: “If I had been a Seriphian, I would not have become so famous; nor would you, had you been fortunate enough to be born an Athenian, have become a Themistocles” (Plato, Republic 329e–330a). But our Jesus was reproached with coming from a village, and that not a Greek village, nor belonging to any nation held in esteem by most people. He was slandered as the son of a poor woman who worked with her hands, and as having left his fatherland because of poverty to work for hire in Egypt. To use the example already given, he was not only a Seriphian, from the smallest and most obscure of islands, but, so to speak, the most low-born of Seriphians. Yet he has been able to stir the whole inhabited world, more than Themistocles the Athenian, and more even than Pythagoras and Plato and any other wise men, kings or generals anywhere in the world.

title: Renowned in every way, despite the cross
english: Who, then, looking into the nature of things with more than passing attention, would not be astonished at him? He conquered, and by his glory he was able to rise above everything that brings disrepute, and above all who were ever renowned. And yet those who have been renowned among men have rarely been able to win glory for several things at once. One was admired and became famous for wisdom, another for generalship; some barbarians for the wonderful powers they worked by incantations; and others for other things, but not for many at once. He, besides everything else, is admired for wisdom, for mighty works, and for his power to lead.

For he won people over not as a tyrant who gets some to join him in revolt against the laws, nor as a brigand who spurs his followers on against other men, nor as a rich man who provides for those who come to him, nor as any of those who are admittedly to be blamed, but as a teacher of the doctrine about the God of the universe, of the worship due to Him, and of a whole way of moral life able to bring whoever lives by it into kinship with the God who is over all.

Nothing ever stood in the way of the glory of Themistocles, or of any other renowned man. But for him, besides the things already mentioned, which were quite enough to hide in obscurity the soul even of a very gifted man, there was also death by crucifixion, which is thought dishonourable. That death was capable of wiping out the glory he had already won, glory that had already taken hold, and of making those who had been deceived before (so those who reject his teaching suppose) abandon the deception and condemn the deceiver.

title: Why the disciples faced death
english: Besides this, one might wonder what moved his disciples, if, as those who speak evil of Jesus say, they had not seen him risen from the dead and had not been persuaded that he was something more divine, not to fear suffering the same things as their teacher, and to meet the danger head-on and leave their homelands to teach, as Jesus willed, the word he had entrusted to them (see Matthew 28:19–20). For I think that anyone who examines the facts fairly would not say that these men gave themselves up to a life full of dangers for the sake of Jesus’ teaching without some great conviction. He had planted it in them by teaching them not only to be shaped by his teachings themselves but also to shape others by them, and to do so when ruin, as far as human life goes, lay in plain view for anyone who dared to bring in new things everywhere and with everyone, and to keep as a friend no one who held fast to his former doctrines and customs.

Did Jesus’ disciples not see this, when they dared to show not only the Jews, from the words of the prophets, that he was the one foretold, but also the other nations that the man crucified only the other day had willingly accepted this death for the human race, like those who died for their countries to put an end to plagues that had taken hold, or famines, or disasters at sea? For it is likely that in the nature of things there is, for certain secret reasons hard for most people to grasp, an order such that one righteous man, dying willingly for the common good, brings about the driving away of evil demons, who cause plagues or famines or disasters at sea or something of the kind.

Let those, then, who wish to disbelieve that Jesus died for mankind by way of the cross tell us: will they also refuse to accept the many Greek and barbarian stories of people who died for the common good, to destroy evils that had already seized cities and nations? Or will they say that those things did happen, but that there is nothing credible in the one they take to be a man dying to destroy a great demon, the ruler of demons, who had made subject to himself all the souls of men that have come to earth?

Jesus’ disciples saw these things, and many more besides, which they are likely to have learned from Jesus in private. They were filled, moreover, with a certain power, since the one who gave them “strength and courage” was not some maiden of the poets but the true understanding and wisdom of God. So they hastened to become “conspicuous among all,” not only among the Argives but among all Greeks and barbarians alike, “and to win noble fame” (Homer, Iliad 5.1–3).

title: The Panthera story and the virgin birth
english: But let us return to the speech Celsus puts in the mouth of his Jew. There the mother of Jesus is described as having been driven out by the carpenter who was betrothed to her, after being convicted of adultery, and as having borne a child by a certain soldier named Panthera. Let us see whether those who made up the tale of the virgin’s adultery with Panthera, and of the carpenter’s driving her out, did not invent all this blindly, in order to overthrow the miraculous conception by the Holy Spirit (Matthew 1:18–20; Luke 1:35). For, because the story was so very wonderful, they could have falsified it in some other way, instead of conceding, as if against their will, that Jesus was not born of an ordinary human marriage. It was to be expected that those who did not accept Jesus’ miraculous birth would invent some lie. But they did not do it convincingly: they held on to the fact that the virgin did not conceive Jesus by Joseph. So, to those able to listen and to expose fabrications, the lie was obvious.

For is it reasonable that he who dared so much for the human race, so that, as far as lay in him, all Greeks and barbarians, looking for divine judgment, might turn away from wickedness and do everything in a way pleasing to the Creator of the universe, should have had no miraculous birth, but the most lawless and shameful birth of all?

I will speak as to Greeks, and especially to Celsus, who, whether he holds these views or not, at any rate cites Plato’s words. Would he who sends souls down into human bodies thrust one who was to dare so much, to teach so many, and to turn many people from the flood of wickedness, into the most shameful birth of all, not even bringing him into human life through lawful marriage? Or is it more reasonable that each soul, for certain secret reasons (I say this now following Pythagoras, Plato and Empedocles, whom Celsus has often named), when it is put into a body, is put there according to its desert and its former character? It is likely, then, that this soul too, which came to dwell in human life and was of more benefit to it than many men (I do not say “all,” so as not to seem to be forcing the argument), needed a body that was not only outstanding among human bodies but the best of all.

title: A soul given a body beyond the ordinary
english: For suppose one soul, for certain hidden reasons, has come to deserve to be neither wholly in the body of a creature without reason nor purely in that of a rational being. It then puts on a misshapen body, so that reason cannot even reach its full growth in one born in that way, whose head is out of proportion to the rest of the body and far too small. Another soul takes on a body such that it becomes a little more rational than the first, and another more rational still, because the nature of the body works, to a greater or lesser degree, against the grasp of reason. If that is so, why should there not also be some soul that takes on a body wholly beyond the ordinary: a body that has something in common with human beings, so that it can live among them, but also something set apart, so that the soul can remain without any taste of evil?

And if the teaching of the physiognomists holds good, whether that of Zopyrus or Loxus or Polemon or of anyone else who has written such things and claimed to know something wonderful, that every body is suited to the character of its soul, then the soul that was to come into human life in an extraordinary way and do great things there had to have a body born, not as Celsus thinks, of Panthera, an adulterer, and a virgin seduced into adultery. For from impure unions like that there should rather have come some senseless teacher, harmful to humankind, teaching licentiousness and injustice and the other vices, not self-control and justice and the other virtues.

title: Isaiah’s prophecy of the virgin
english: Rather, as the prophets also foretold, it had to come from a virgin who, according to the promise of a sign, would give birth to one named after a fact, a fact which showed that at his birth God would be with human beings (Isaiah 7:14).

And it seems to me fitting, in answer to the Jew whom Celsus impersonates, to set out the prophecy of Isaiah, which says that Emmanuel would be born of a virgin. Celsus did not quote it. Either he did not know it, for all that he professes to know everything, or he had read it and chose to keep silent, so as not to seem to be unwittingly building up an argument that tells against his own purpose. The passage reads as follows: “And the Lord spoke again to Ahaz, saying: Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, in the depth or in the height. And Ahaz said: I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test. And he said: Hear then, house of David: is it a small thing for you to make trouble for men? And how is it that you make trouble for the Lord? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: Behold, the virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel” (Isaiah 7:10–14), which is interpreted “God with us” (Matthew 1:23).

That Celsus left the prophecy out in bad faith is clear to me from this: he cites a great deal from the Gospel according to Matthew, such as the star that rose at the birth of Jesus (Matthew 2:2) and other wonders, yet he makes no mention of this at all. But if a Jew quibbles and says that the text does not read “Behold, the virgin” but instead “Behold, the young woman,” we shall reply to him that the word aalma, which the Seventy rendered “the virgin” and others “the young woman,” also occurs, so they say, in Deuteronomy of a virgin, as follows: “If there is a girl, a virgin, betrothed to a man, and a man finds her in the city and lies with her, you shall bring them both out to the gate of their city, and they shall be stoned with stones and shall die: the young woman because she did not cry out in the city, and the man because he dishonoured his neighbour’s wife” (Deuteronomy 22:23–24). And next: “But if a man finds the betrothed girl in the field, and the man forces her and lies with her, you shall put to death only the man who lay with her, and to the young woman you shall do nothing; the young woman has committed no sin deserving death” (Deuteronomy 22:25–26).

title: The sign given to the house of David
english: But so that we may not seem to rest on a Hebrew word, offering people who cannot tell whether to accept it or not our proof that the prophet said this child would be born of a virgin, the child of whose birth the words “God with us” have been spoken, let us make the point good from the wording itself. The Lord is recorded as having said to Ahaz: “Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, in the depth or in the height” (Isaiah 7:11), and next comes the sign that is given: “Behold, the virgin shall be with child and bear a son” (Isaiah 7:14). What sort of sign, then, would it be for a young woman who was not a virgin to give birth? And to whom is it more fitting to bear “Emmanuel,” that is, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23)? To a woman who has had intercourse and conceived through a woman’s passion, or to one still pure and chaste and a virgin? For it is fitting for her to bring forth the offspring at whose birth it is said, “God with us.”

And if he quibbles in this way too, saying that the words “Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God” were spoken to Ahaz, we shall answer: who was born in the time of Ahaz at whose birth it is said, “Emmanuel, which is, God with us”? For if no one is to be found, then clearly what was said to Ahaz was said to the house of David (Isaiah 7:13), because the Saviour is recorded to have come “from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3). Moreover, this sign is said to be “in the depth or in the height,” since “he who descended is the very one who also ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things” (Ephesians 4:10). I say this as to a Jew who accepts the prophecy.

But let Celsus too, or any of his party, say with what kind of mind the prophet speaks of the future, in these words or in any of the others recorded in the prophecies. Is it a mind that foreknows the future, or not? If it foreknows the future, the prophets had a divine Spirit. If it does not foreknow the future, let him explain the mind of a man who ventures to speak about the future and is admired among the Jews for prophecy.

title: Why the Jews needed prophets
english: Now that we have come to the subject of the prophets, what we are about to bring forward will not be without use to the Jews, who believe that the prophets spoke by a divine Spirit, nor to fair-minded Greeks either. To them we shall say that one must accept that the Jews too had prophets, if they were to be kept within the law given them, to believe in the Creator as they had received him, and, as far as the law was concerned, to have no occasion to fall away into the many gods of the nations. We shall show this necessity as follows. “The nations,” as is written in the very law of the Jews, “will listen to omens and divinations” (Deuteronomy 18:14); but to that people it is said, “But to you the Lord your God has not granted it so” (Deuteronomy 18:14). And to this is added, “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers” (Deuteronomy 18:15).

The nations, then, used divination by “omens,” or by augury, or by birds, or by mediums, or by those who profess the art of reading sacrifices, or by Chaldeans who cast nativities, all of which were forbidden to the Jews (Deuteronomy 18:10–11). If the Jews had had no comfort from knowledge of the future, the mere human craving to know what is to come would have led them to despise what was their own, as having nothing divine in it. They would not have received any prophet after Moses, nor written down the prophets’ words, but would have deserted to the oracles and oracle-shrines of the nations, or else tried to set up something of the kind among themselves. So it is not at all strange that their prophets foretold even ordinary matters, to comfort those who longed for such things: so that Samuel prophesied even “about lost asses” (1 Samuel 9:20), and the prophet recorded in First Kings prophesied about the illness of a king’s son (1 Kings 14:1–13). And how could the champions of the Jewish law have rebuked anyone who wanted to get divination from idols? Elijah, for instance, is found rebuking Ahaziah and saying, “Is it because there is no God in Israel that you go to inquire of Baal the Fly, the god of Ekron?” (2 Kings 1:3).

title: The virgin birth and the Greeks’ own stories
english: It seems to me, then, that a fair case has been made, not only that our Saviour was to be born of a virgin, but also that there were prophets among the Jews. They foretold not only general things about the future, such as those concerning Christ, the kingdoms of the world, what would befall Israel, the nations that would believe in the Saviour, and many other things said about him, but also particular things: how the lost asses of Kish would be found (1 Samuel 9:3–20), the illness from which the son of the king of Israel was suffering (1 Kings 14:1–13), or anything else of the kind on record.

Further, to Greeks who refuse to believe in the birth of Jesus from a virgin, this must be said. In the generation of the various living creatures the Creator showed that, if he willed, he could do in other creatures, and in human beings themselves, what he does in a single kind of creature. Some female creatures are found that have no union with a male, as writers on animals say of vultures; this creature keeps up the succession of its kind without mating. What is so extraordinary, then, if God, wishing to send a divine teacher to the human race, caused the formative principle of the child to be born to come about in another way, instead of through the seminal principle that comes from the union of men with women?

And even by the account of the Greeks themselves, not all human beings were born of a man and a woman. For if the world had a beginning, as many of the Greeks also held, the first human beings must have come into being not from intercourse but from the earth, when seminal principles took form in the earth. And this, I think, is more extraordinary than that Jesus should have been born half in the same way as the rest of humankind.

There is nothing out of place in using Greek stories too in answering Greeks, so that we may not seem to be the only ones to make use of this extraordinary story. For some have seen fit to record, not only about ancient and heroic tales but also about people of yesterday and the day before, that it was possible that Plato too was born of Amphictione, Ariston being prevented from having union with her until she had given birth to the child begotten by Apollo. But these are truly myths, and they moved people to invent such a story about a man whom they thought to have greater wisdom and power than most, and to have received the first formation of his body from higher and more divine seed, since this befits those who are greater than human.

But since Celsus has brought in his Jew arguing with Jesus and ridiculing what Celsus takes to be the pretence of his birth from a virgin, and adducing the Greek myths about Danae, Melanippe, Auge and Antiope, it must be said that such words befitted a buffoon, not a man in earnest about what he reports.

title: The charge of magic learned in Egypt
english: Next he takes the account written in the Gospel according to Matthew of Jesus' journey into Egypt (Matthew 2:13–15). He does not believe the miraculous part of it, either that an angel gave the command for it, or whether Jesus' leaving Judea and staying in Egypt hinted at some hidden meaning. Instead he has made up another story. In a way he grants the miraculous works that Jesus did, by which he persuaded the many to follow him as Christ; but he wants to slander them as done by magic and not by divine power. For he says that “he was brought up in obscurity, went to Egypt to work for hire, tried his hand there at certain powers, and came back from there proclaiming himself God on the strength of those powers.”

For my part, I do not know how a magician would have laboured to teach a doctrine that persuades people to do everything in the belief that God will judge each person for all that he has done, and that shapes in this way his own disciples, whom he meant to use as ministers of his teaching. Did they too, having been taught in this way to work miracles, win over those who heard them, or did they not work miracles at all? To say that they worked no miracles at all, but that, once they believed, they gave themselves to teaching a new doctrine to whomever they came among, without any skill in speech comparable to the dialectical wisdom of the Greeks, is wholly unreasonable. For in what did they trust when they taught the doctrine and brought in something new? But if they too performed miracles, what likelihood is there that magicians would have exposed themselves to such great dangers for a teaching that forbids magic?

title: Mockery about the mother of Jesus
english: I do not think I need contend with an argument put forward not in earnest but in mockery: “Was the mother of Jesus beautiful, then, and did God have intercourse with her because she was beautiful, though it is not his nature to love a perishable body?” Or that “it was not even likely that God would fall in love with her, since she was neither wealthy nor of royal birth; for no one knew her, not even her neighbours.” He is joking too when he says that “when she was hated by the carpenter and driven out, neither divine power nor persuasive speech saved her.” “These things, then,” he says, “have nothing to do with the kingdom of God.” How would such remarks differ from those of people who hurl abuse at others at the crossroads and say nothing worth serious attention?

title: Celsus attacks without order
english: After this he takes from the Gospel according to Matthew, and perhaps also from the other Gospels, the account of the dove that alighted on the Saviour when he was being baptized by John (Matthew 3:16), and wants to slander what is said as a fiction. Having ridiculed, as he supposed, the account of our Saviour's birth from a virgin, he does not set out what comes next in its order. For anger and hatred have nothing orderly about them; people who are angry and hostile abuse those they hate as things occur to them, since their passion does not allow them to state their charges with reflection and in order. If he had kept to the order, he would have taken up the Gospel and, having set himself to accuse it, would have attacked the first account and then gone on in turn to the second, and so to the rest. But as it is, Celsus, who professes to know everything about us, after the birth from a virgin brings charges against the Holy Spirit who appeared at the baptism in the form of a dove; then after this he slanders the prophecy of our Saviour's coming; and after that he runs back to what is recorded next after the birth of Jesus, the story of the star and of the magi who came from the east “to worship” the child (Matthew 2:1–2).

If you watch for it yourself, you could find many things said by Celsus in confusion throughout his whole book, so that by this too he may be convicted, before those who know how to keep order and to look for it, of having given his book the title True Doctrine with great rashness and boasting, a thing that none of the philosophers of repute did. For Plato says that it is not the part of a man of sense to insist firmly on such matters, and on others still more obscure (Plato, Phaedo 114d); and Chrysippus, after setting out in many places the reasons that moved him, sends us on to any we may find who will speak better than he. This man, then, wiser both than these and than the rest of the Greeks, in keeping with his claim to know everything, gave his book the title True Doctrine.

title: The Jew mocks the dove at the baptism
english: But so that we may not seem to pass over his main points on purpose, for lack of an answer, we have decided to answer, as well as we can, each of the things he puts forward, paying attention not to the natural connection and sequence of the subjects but to the order of what is written in his book. Come, then, let us see what he says in slandering the Holy Spirit, seen by the Saviour, as it were bodily, in the form of a dove (Luke 3:22). It is still his Jew who says these things, speaking to the one whom we confess to be our Lord, Jesus: “When you were bathing beside John,” he says, “you say that an apparition of a bird flew down on you out of the air.” Then the Jew he has brought in goes on to ask: “What credible witness saw this apparition, or who heard a voice from heaven adopting you as God's Son (Matthew 3:17)? Except that you say so, and bring in one of those who were punished along with you.”

title: How histories are to be read
english: Before we begin our defence, it must be said that to try to establish that almost any story, even a true one, actually happened, and to produce a certain and convincing impression about it, is among the very hardest of tasks, and in some cases impossible. Suppose someone says that the Trojan War did not happen, chiefly because an impossible tale has been woven into it, that a certain Achilles was born the son of a sea goddess, Thetis, and of a man, Peleus, or Sarpedon the son of Zeus, or Ascalaphus and Ialmenus the sons of Ares, or Aeneas the son of Aphrodite. How could we establish such a thing, especially when we are hard pressed by the fiction that has somehow been woven into the opinion, held by everyone, that the war at Ilium between the Greeks and the Trojans really happened? Suppose, too, someone disbelieves the story of Oedipus and Jocasta and of Eteocles and Polynices, who were born of them both, because the Sphinx, a kind of half-maiden, has been woven into the tale. How could we prove such a thing? So too with the story of the Epigoni, even though nothing of the kind is woven into it, or with the return of the Heraclidae, or with countless others.
