But one who reads histories with fairness, and who wants to keep himself from being deceived even in them, will judge which things he will assent to, which he will take figuratively, searching out the intention of those who invented such things, and which he will disbelieve as written to please certain people. And we have said this in advance with the whole account of Jesus found in the Gospels in view. We are not calling the more intelligent to a bare and unreasoning faith; we want to show that those who are to read them need fairness, much examination, and, if I may call it so, an entering into the intention of the writers, so that it may be found in what sense each thing has been written.

title: The Jew believes greater wonders in the prophets
english: First, then, we shall say this. If the man who disbelieves the apparition of the Holy Spirit in the form of the dove had been represented as an Epicurean, or a follower of Democritus, or a Peripatetic, what is said would have fitted the character being portrayed. But as it is, the most wise Celsus has not seen even this: that he has put such an argument in the mouth of a Jew, who believes things from the prophetic Scriptures more numerous and more marvellous than the story of the form of the dove. For someone might say to the Jew, who disbelieves the apparition and thinks he can accuse it as a fiction: And you, sir, how could you prove that the Lord God said to Adam, or to Eve, or to Cain, or to Noah, or to Abraham, or to Isaac, or to Jacob the things that are recorded as said by him to these men (Genesis 2:16; 3:13; 4:6; 6:13; 12:1; 26:2; 28:13)?

And to set one story beside another, I would say to the Jew: Your own Ezekiel too wrote, saying, “The heavens were opened, and I saw a vision of God” (Ezekiel 1:1); and having described it he adds, “This was the vision of the likeness of the glory of the Lord; and he said to me” (Ezekiel 1:28; 2:1). For if what is recorded about Jesus is false, since we cannot, as you suppose, clearly show how these things are true, which were seen or heard by him alone and, as you thought you had noticed, by one of those who were punished, why shall we not all the more say that Ezekiel too was telling marvels when he said, “The heavens were opened,” and the rest? Again, when Isaiah says, “I saw the Lord of Hosts sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and the Seraphim stood around him, six wings to the one and six wings to the other” (Isaiah 6:1–2), and the rest, how do you know that he truly saw it? For you, Jew, have believed these things as free of falsehood, and as things that, by a more divine Spirit, were not only seen by the prophet but also spoken and written down.

Who is more worthy of belief when he says that the heavens were opened to him and that he heard a voice, or that he saw “the Lord of Hosts sitting on a throne, high and lifted up” (Isaiah 6:1): Isaiah and Ezekiel, or Jesus? For no work of theirs so great is to be found; but the noble work of Jesus did not take place only in the days when he lived in the body. Even to this day the power of Jesus is at work, bringing about conversion and amendment of life in those who believe in God through him. And a clear proof that these things happen by his power is this: though, as he himself says and as one can see, there are no labourers to work at the harvest of souls (Matthew 9:37–38), so great a harvest is being gathered in and brought together into God's threshing floors and churches everywhere.

title: The Spirit taught the Gospel writers
english: I say these things to the Jew not because I, a Christian, disbelieve Ezekiel and Isaiah, but to shame him by what we both believe: that this man is far more worthy than they are to be believed when he says that he saw such things and, as is likely, handed on to his disciples the vision he saw and the voice he heard. Someone else might say that not all of those who recorded the story of the form of the dove and of the voice from heaven heard Jesus tell of these things, but that the Spirit who taught Moses the history older than himself, beginning from the making of the world and reaching to the times of Abraham, his forefather, also taught those who wrote the Gospel the wonder that took place at the time of Jesus' baptism.

And the one who has been graced with the gift called “the word of wisdom” (1 Corinthians 12:8) will also explain the reason for the opening of the heavens and for the form of the dove, and why the Holy Spirit appeared to Jesus in the form of this living creature and not of any other. But our argument does not now require us to explain this. For the point in hand is to show that Celsus did not act soundly in putting into a Jew's mouth, with words like these, disbelief about an event that is more likely to have happened than the things the Jew himself believes.

title: A debate with Jewish teachers about Moses and Jesus
english: I remember that once, in a debate with some Jews who were said to be wise, with a good many people judging what was said, I used an argument of this kind:

Tell me, sirs: two men have come to live among the human race about whom marvellous things, beyond human nature, are recorded. I mean Moses, your lawgiver, who wrote about himself, and Jesus, our teacher, who left no writing of his own about himself but is attested by his disciples in the Gospels. By what arbitrary choice is Moses to be believed as telling the truth, even though the Egyptians slander him as a sorcerer who seemed to have worked his mighty deeds by trickery, while Jesus is to be disbelieved because you accuse him? For whole peoples bear witness to both: Jews to Moses; and Christians, who do not deny the prophecy of Moses but prove from it the things concerning Jesus, accept as true the marvels about Jesus recorded by his disciples.

For if you demand from us an account of Jesus, first give one of Moses, who came before him; then we in turn will give ours of Jesus. But since you shrink back and run from the proofs about Moses, for the present we do the same as you and offer no proof. Nonetheless, admit that you have no demonstration about Moses, and hear the proofs about Jesus from the law and the prophets. And here is the marvel: from the proofs about Jesus in the law and the prophets it is proved that both Moses and the prophets were prophets of God.

title: Signs of the Spirit who came as a dove
english: The law and the prophets are full of marvels like the one recorded about Jesus at his baptism, concerning the dove and the voice from heaven (Matthew 3:16–17; Mark 1:10–11; Luke 3:21–22). And I think that the marvels Jesus performed are a sign that the Holy Spirit was then seen in the form of a dove; Celsus slanders these, saying that he learned them among the Egyptians and so performed them. I will appeal not to those alone but also, as is reasonable, to the ones the apostles of Jesus performed. For without mighty works and marvels they would not have moved those who heard new doctrines and new teachings to leave their ancestral ways and to accept these men's teachings at the risk even of death. And traces of that Holy Spirit who was seen in the form of a dove are still preserved among Christians. They drive out demons, perform many healings, and, as the Word wills, see certain things about the future.

Celsus may mock what I am about to say, or the Jew he has brought in may, but it shall be said all the same: many have come to Christianity as if against their will. Some spirit suddenly turned their ruling mind from hating the message to dying for it, and showed them visions, waking or in dreams. For we have learned of many such things; and if we, who were present ourselves and saw them, were to write them down, we would draw loud laughter from unbelievers, who think that we too, like those they suppose to have made up these things, are making them up. But God is witness to our conscience, which wishes to commend the divine teaching of Jesus not by false reports but by clear evidence of many kinds.

But since it is a Jew who raises difficulties about the Holy Spirit, recorded to have come down upon Jesus in the form of a dove, we should say to him: Sir, who is it that says in Isaiah, “And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isaiah 48:16)? Since the phrase there is ambiguous, whether the Father and the Holy Spirit sent Jesus, or the Father sent both Christ and the Holy Spirit, the second is true. And since the Saviour was sent, and then the Holy Spirit, so that what was spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled, and the fulfilment of the prophecy had to be made known to those who came after as well, for this reason the disciples of Jesus recorded what took place.

title: Josephus on John the Baptist and James
english: I should have liked to say to Celsus, who presents his Jew as somehow accepting John as a Baptist who baptized Jesus, that the fact that John was a Baptist, baptizing for the forgiveness of sins (Mark 1:4), was recorded by one who lived not long after John and Jesus. For in the eighteenth book of his Jewish Antiquities Josephus bears witness to John as a Baptist who promised purification to those who were baptized (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 18.116–119). This same writer, though he did not believe in Jesus as the Christ, was looking for the cause of the fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of the temple. He ought to have said that the plot against Jesus was the cause of these things for the people, because they killed the Christ who had been foretold. Yet, as if against his will, he came not far from the truth, and says that these things befell the Jews to avenge James the Just, who was the brother of “Jesus who is called Christ,” since they killed him although he was most just.

This James is the one whom Paul, a true disciple of Jesus, says he saw, calling him “the Lord's brother” (Galatians 1:19), not so much because of kinship by blood or their shared upbringing as because of his character and his teaching. If, then, Josephus says that the desolation of Jerusalem befell the Jews because of James, is it not more reasonable to say that it happened because of Jesus the Christ? Witnesses to his divinity are the churches, so many in number, of those who have turned from the flood of evils, who cling to the Creator and refer everything to pleasing him.

title: The divine senses and the opened heavens
english: Even if the Jew, then, will not make a defence for Ezekiel and Isaiah when we place side by side the opening of the heavens for Jesus, with the voice he heard, and the like things we find recorded in Ezekiel and in Isaiah (Ezekiel 1:1; Isaiah 6:1–2) or in some other prophet, we at least will support our case as best we can. We say that, just as it is believed that many have had visions in dreams, some of more divine things, others telling of future events of this life, whether clearly or in riddles, and this is plain to all who accept providence, so what is absurd in holding that what forms impressions on the ruling mind in a dream can form them on it while awake as well, for the benefit of the one in whom they are formed, or of those who will hear of them from him? And just as in a dream we have the impression that we hear and that our bodily ear is struck, and that we see with our eyes, though neither the eyes of the body nor the hearing is being struck, but the ruling mind is undergoing these things, so there is nothing absurd in such things having happened to the prophets, when it is recorded that they saw certain quite extraordinary things, or heard words of the Lord, or beheld the heavens opening. For I do not suppose that the visible heaven was opened, and its body split apart as it opened, so that Ezekiel might record such a thing.

Perhaps, then, in the case of the Saviour too, whoever listens to the Gospels with understanding should take it in the same way, even if such a view offends the simpler sort, who in their great simplicity set the universe moving, splitting the vast, unified body of the whole heaven. But one who examines the matter more deeply will say this. There is, as Scripture has named it, a divine sense, general in kind, which only the blessed man finds even now, according to what is said in Solomon too: “You will find a divine sense” (Proverbs 2:5). This sense has its kinds: a sight naturally able to see things higher than bodies, among which the cherubim or the seraphim are shown (Ezekiel 10:1; Isaiah 6:2); a hearing that receives voices whose being is not in the air; a taste that feeds on living bread, which has come down from heaven and gives life to the world (John 6:33, 51); so too a smell that smells such things as Paul means when he speaks of being “the aroma of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2:15); and a touch, by which John says he has handled with his hands “the Word of life” (1 John 1:1). The blessed prophets found this divine sense. They saw in a divine way and heard in a divine way, and tasted and smelled in the same way, by a sense that, if I may so name it, is not of the senses; and they touched the Word with faith, so that an outflow from him came to them to heal them. In this way they saw what they record that they saw, and heard what they say they heard, and had the like experiences as they wrote of them, eating the “roll” of a book that was given to them (Ezekiel 2:9–3:3).

So too Isaac “smelled the smell of” his son's more divine “garments,” and spoke these words as a spiritual blessing: “See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a full field, which the Lord has blessed” (Genesis 27:27). In a like way, Jesus “touched” the leper (Matthew 8:3) with a touch of the mind rather than of the senses, to cleanse him, as I think, in two ways: he freed him not only, as most people take it, from bodily leprosy by a bodily touch, but also from the other leprosy by his truly divine touch.

It was in this way, then, that “John bore witness, saying: ‘I have seen the Spirit descending as a dove from heaven, and it remained on him. And I did not know him; but he who sent me to baptize in water said to me, “He on whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining on him, this is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.” And I have seen, and have borne witness that this is the Son of God’” (John 1:32–34). And for Jesus the heavens were opened (Matthew 3:16), and at that time no one but John is recorded to have seen the heavens opened. But the Saviour, foretelling to his disciples that this opening of the heavens would come, and that they would see it, says: “Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (John 1:51). And so Paul was caught up to the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:2), having first seen it opened, since he was a disciple of Jesus. But to explain now why Paul says, “Whether in the body I do not know, or out of the body I do not know; God knows” (2 Corinthians 12:2), does not belong to the present occasion.

Further, I will add to my argument the very point Celsus assumes: that Jesus himself told of the opening of the heavens and of the Holy Spirit that came down upon him in the form of a dove at the Jordan, although Scripture does not present him as saying that he saw this. This most noble man did not see that it does not fit the one who said to his disciples about the vision on the mountain, “Tell the vision to no one until the Son of Man has risen from the dead” (Matthew 17:9), to have told his disciples what John saw and heard at the Jordan. One may see this also in the character of Jesus, who everywhere avoided speaking about himself and for that reason said, “Even if I speak about myself, my testimony is not true” (John 5:31). And since he avoided speaking about himself, and wished to show that he was the Christ by his deeds rather than by his words, for this reason the Jews say to him, “If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John 10:24).

But since it is a Jew in Celsus who says to Jesus, about the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove, “Except that you say so, and bring forward one of those who were punished with you,” we must show Celsus that this too he has not fittingly attributed to the Jewish character. For the Jews do not link John with Jesus, nor John's punishment with the punishment of Jesus. In this too, then, the man who boasted that he knew everything stands convicted, for he did not know what words to give the Jewish character in addressing Jesus.

title: Celsus passes over the prophecies
english: After this, I do not know how, he willingly passes over the most important point in the case for Jesus: that he was foretold by the prophets of the Jews, by Moses and those after him, and even by those before Moses. I think he does so because he cannot answer the argument, any more than the Jews can, or the sects that do not want Jesus to have been foretold. Perhaps he did not even know the prophecies about Jesus. For had he taken up what Christians say, that many prophets foretold the Saviour's coming, he would not have put into the mouth of his Jew words that would have suited a Samaritan or a Sadducee better. Nor would the Jew of his invented speech have said: "But a prophet of mine once said in Jerusalem that a Son of God will come, judge of the holy and punisher of the unrighteous."

For it was not just one prophet who foretold the things about Christ. And even if the Samaritans or the Sadducees, who accept only the books of Moses, were to say that the Christ was foretold in those books, still the prophecy was certainly not spoken in Jerusalem, which had not yet been named in the time of Moses.

If only, then, all who accuse our teaching were as ignorant as this, not only of the facts but even of the bare letter of Scripture, and accused Christianity in that state, so that their argument might lack even ordinary persuasiveness, the kind able to draw away the unsteady and those who believe "for a while" (Luke 8:13), not from faith but from little faith.

But a Jew would not admit that any prophet said that a Son of God would come. What they say is that the Christ of God will come. And indeed they often argue with us straight away about the Son of God, as though there were no such being and none had been foretold. We are not saying that a Son of God is not foretold, but that Celsus has given the Jewish character, who does not admit any such thing, words that do not fit him: "A prophet of mine once said in Jerusalem that a Son of God will come."

title: Prophets spoke of Christ in many ways
english: Then, as though this alone had been foretold, that he would be judge of the holy and punisher of the unrighteous, and as though neither the place of his birth, nor the suffering he would undergo at the hands of the Jews, nor his resurrection, nor the wonderful works of power he would do had been foretold, he says: "Why should you, rather than the countless others who have lived after the prophecy, be the one about whom these things were foretold?" And, I do not know how, wishing to allow that others too might be suspected of being the ones foretold, he says that "some in a frenzy and others going about begging say that a Son of God has come from above." For we have not found it recorded that the Jews admit such things to have happened.

First, then, it must be said that many prophets foretold the things about Christ in every kind of way: some through riddles, others through allegory or in some other manner, and some even in so many words. Later on, in the speech he gives his Jew addressed to those of his own people who believe, he says that the prophecies referred to the events of Jesus' life can be fitted to other events as well. Since he says this cleverly and with ill intent, we shall set out a few prophecies out of many. Let anyone who wishes say something compelling against them to overthrow them, something able to move those who believe with understanding away from the faith.

title: Bethlehem foretold and remembered
english: About the place of his birth it has been said that "the ruler will come forth" (Matthew 2:6) from "Bethlehem," in this way: "And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, are small indeed to be among the thousands of Judah; out of you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, and his goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity" (Micah 5:2). This prophecy would fit none of those who, as Celsus's Jew says, are in a frenzy and go about begging and say they have come from above, unless he were clearly shown to have been born in Bethlehem, or, as someone else might put it, to have come from Bethlehem to lead the people.

As for Jesus' birth in Bethlehem, if anyone wants to be persuaded from other sources as well, besides Micah's prophecy and the account recorded in the Gospels by Jesus' disciples, let him consider this. In keeping with the Gospel account of his birth, the cave in Bethlehem where he was born is shown, and the manger in the cave where he was wrapped in swaddling cloths (Luke 2:7). And what is shown there is widely known in those parts, even among those who are strangers to the faith: that in this cave was born the Jesus whom Christians worship and admire.

For my part, I think that before Christ's coming the chief priests and scribes of the people taught that the Christ would be born in Bethlehem, because the prophecy was clear and plain. And this teaching reached the mass of the Jews as well. That is why Herod is recorded to have heard from the chief priests and scribes of the people, when he inquired of them, that the Christ would be born "in Bethlehem of Judea" (Matthew 2:4-5), the town David came from. Further, in the Gospel according to John it is said that Jews stated that the Christ would be born in Bethlehem, the town David came from (John 7:42).

But after Christ's coming, those who set to work to destroy the belief that his birth had been foretold long before removed this teaching from the people. In this they did something much like those who won over the soldiers of the guard at the tomb, who had seen him risen from the dead and were reporting it, and who said to those who had seen it: "Say that his disciples stole him by night while we were asleep. And if this is heard before the governor, we will do the persuading and keep you free of trouble" (Matthew 28:13-14).

title: Why habit blinds people to plain proof
english: For contentiousness and prejudice are a hard thing. They can make people set themselves even against what is evident, so that they will not give up doctrines which have dyed them indelibly, to which they have somehow grown used, and which have coloured their souls. A man would more easily give up his habits in other matters, even if he finds it hard to tear himself from them, than those that concern doctrines. Yet even those other habits are not easily set aside by those used to them. So people who have grown attached to houses, or cities or villages, or familiar companions, are not readily willing to leave them.

This, then, was the reason why many of the Jews at that time also set themselves against the plain evidence of the prophecies and of the wonders that Jesus did and is recorded to have undergone. That human nature is affected in some such way will be clear to those who observe how people once taken up even with the most shameful and senseless traditions of their fathers and fellow citizens are not easily moved from them. One would not quickly persuade an Egyptian, at any rate, to despise what he has received from his fathers, so that he would no longer think this or that irrational animal a god, or no longer guard himself, even at the cost of his life, from tasting the flesh of this or that animal.

So if, in examining this argument, we have gone through the matter of Bethlehem and the prophecy about it at some length, we think we have done so of necessity. We were answering those who might say: if the prophecies about Jesus among the Jews were so plain, why ever did they not assent to his teaching when he came, and go over to the better things that Jesus showed? But let no one bring the like reproach against those of us who believe, seeing that arguments by no means contemptible are put forward for faith in Jesus by those who have learned to champion them.

title: The ruler from Judah and the hope of the nations
english: And if a second prophecy about Jesus is needed, one that seems to us plain, we shall set out the one written by Moses very many years before Jesus' coming. Moses says that Jacob, as he was departing this life, prophesied to each of his sons (Genesis 49:1), and said to Judah, among other things: "A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until the things laid up for him come" (Genesis 49:10).

Anyone who reads this prophecy, which in truth is much older than Moses, though one of the unbelievers might suppose it was spoken by Moses, would wonder how Moses could have foretold that the kings of the Jews, though there were twelve tribes among them, would be born of the tribe of Judah and would rule the people. That is why the whole people are called Jews, taking their name from the ruling tribe.

And one who reads the prophecy fair-mindedly would wonder at it a second time: how, having said that the rulers and leaders of the people would come from the tribe of Judah, he also fixed the end of their rule, saying that a ruler would not fail "from Judah," nor a leader "from his thighs, until the things laid up for him come, and he is the expectation of the nations" (Genesis 49:10). For he has come to whom "the things laid up" belong, the Christ of God, "the ruler" of God's promises. And he alone, beyond all who were before him, and I would boldly say beyond all who came after him too, has clearly become "the expectation of the nations." For people from all the nations have believed in God through him, and, as Isaiah said, the nations have hoped in his name; for he said: "In his name the nations will hope" (Isaiah 42:4).

He also said "Come out" "to those in bonds," since "each one is bound fast by the cords of his own sins" (Proverbs 5:22), and he told those in ignorance to come into the light. These things too were foretold, in this way: "And I have given you as a covenant of the nations, to establish the earth and to inherit a desolate inheritance, saying to those in bonds, Come out, and to those in darkness, Show yourselves" (Isaiah 49:8-9). And at his coming one can see fulfilled, in the simpler believers all over the world, the words: "And in all the ways they shall feed, and in all the paths shall be their pasture" (Isaiah 49:9).

title: The Servant’s suffering foretold by Isaiah
english: Celsus, who professes to know everything about our teaching, reproaches the Saviour over his suffering, as though he had not been helped by the Father or had not been able to help himself. We must therefore show that his suffering was foretold together with its cause: that it was to the profit of mankind that he should die for them and suffer the bruise that came with his condemnation (Isaiah 53:5). It had also been foretold that those from the nations, among whom the prophets had not arisen, "will understand" him (Isaiah 52:15), and it had been said that he would be seen with a "form without honour" in the sight of men (Isaiah 53:3). The text runs thus:

"Behold, my servant shall understand, and he shall be exalted and glorified and lifted up exceedingly. Just as many shall be astonished at you, so shall your form be held in no esteem by men, and your glory by men. So shall many nations marvel at him, and kings shall shut their mouths; for those to whom nothing was announced about him shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand" (Isaiah 52:13-15).

"Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? We announced him as a little child before him, as a root in a thirsty land. He has no form nor glory; and we saw him, and he had no form nor beauty. But his form was without honour and fell short of all men's: a man under the stroke, and knowing how to bear weakness, for his face is turned away. He was dishonoured and held of no account. He bears our sins and suffers pain for us, and we reckoned him to be in toil and under the stroke and in affliction. But he was wounded because of our sins and made weak because of our lawless deeds; the chastisement that brings us peace was upon him; by his bruise we were healed. All of us went astray like sheep; each man went astray in his own way; and the Lord gave him up for our sins. And he, because he has been afflicted, does not open his mouth. As a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and as a lamb is silent before its shearer, so he does not open his mouth. In his humiliation his judgement was taken away. Who shall tell of his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth; because of the lawless deeds of my people he was led to death" (Isaiah 53:1-8).

title: The suffering servant is not the whole people
english: I remember once using these prophecies in a debate with those whom the Jews call wise. To this the Jew replied that they had been prophesied of the whole people as of a single person, a people that had been in the dispersion and had been struck, so that many might become proselytes through the Jews having been scattered among the other nations. In this way he explained “Your appearance will be without honour among men” (Isaiah 52:14), and “Those who were not told of him will see” (Isaiah 52:15), and “a man under a blow” (Isaiah 53:3).

Many arguments were put forward in that debate to prove that they have no good reason for referring to the whole people these prophecies, which concern one particular person. I asked whose character it could be that says, “This man bears our sins and suffers pain for us” (Isaiah 53:4), and, “But he was wounded because of our sins, and has been made weak because of our lawless deeds” (Isaiah 53:5); and whose character it was that declares, “By his bruise we were healed” (Isaiah 53:5). For plainly it is those who had been in sins and were healed through the Saviour’s suffering, whether they came from that people or from the nations, who say these words in the prophet, who foresaw this and, by the Holy Spirit, put these words in their mouths.

But we seemed to press them hardest with the passage that says, “Because of the lawless deeds of my people he was led to death” (Isaiah 53:8). For if, on their view, it is the people who are the subject of the prophecy, how is this man said to have been led “to death” “because of the lawless deeds of the people” of God, unless he is someone other than the people of God? And who is he, if not Jesus Christ, by whose “bruise” we who believe in him “were healed” (Isaiah 53:5; 1 Peter 2:24), he who stripped off “the rulers and authorities” that were in us, and made a show of them “openly” on the tree (Colossians 2:15)?

To make clear each point in the prophecy, and to leave none of it unexamined, belongs to another occasion. Even this much has been said at some length, necessarily, I think, because of the words of Celsus’s Jew quoted above.

title: Two comings of Christ and the God who is anointed
english: Celsus and his Jew, and all who have not believed in Jesus, have failed to notice that the prophecies speak of two comings of Christ. The first is more subject to human sufferings and more lowly, so that Christ, being with human beings, might teach the way that leads to God, and might leave no one in this human life any room to plead that he had not known of the judgment to come. The other is glorious and wholly divine, with nothing of human suffering woven into its divinity.

To set out the prophecies would take a long time. For the present it is enough to take the passage from the forty-fourth Psalm (Psalm 45 in English Bibles), which, among other things, bears the title “A song for the beloved” (Psalm 45, title). There he is also plainly proclaimed God, in these words: “Grace has been poured out on your lips; therefore God has blessed you for ever. Gird your sword on your thigh, O mighty one, in your loveliness and your beauty; and bend your bow, and prosper, and reign, for the sake of truth and meekness and righteousness, and your right hand will guide you wonderfully. Your arrows are sharpened, O mighty one; peoples will fall beneath you; in the heart of the king’s enemies” (Psalm 45:2–5).

Pay careful attention to what comes next, where he is called God. “Your throne,” it says, “O God, is for ever and ever; a rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 45:6–7). Notice that the prophet, addressing God, whose “throne” is “for ever and ever,” and the rod of whose kingdom is “a rod of uprightness,” says that this God has been anointed by God, who was his God; and that he was anointed because he, above his “companions,” loved “righteousness” and hated “lawlessness” (Psalm 45:7).

And I remember pressing the Jew who was thought wise very hard with this passage. At a loss before it, he said what fitted his own Judaism: he said that “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; a rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom” (Psalm 45:6) was spoken to the God of the universe, and that “You have loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you” (Psalm 45:7), and what follows, was spoken to the Christ.

title: True sonship and those who falsely claimed it
english: Again, his Jew says to the Saviour: “If you say this, that every human being who has come into being by divine providence is a son of God, how would you differ from anyone else?” To him we shall reply that everyone who is no longer schooled by fear, but chooses the good for its own sake, is, as Paul named him, a son of God. But the Saviour differs greatly, and by a long way, from everyone who is called a son of God because of virtue, for he is, as it were, a kind of spring and source of all such. Paul’s words run like this: “For you did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you received a spirit of adoption, in which we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15).

“Some, too,” as Celsus’s Jew says, “countless people, will refute Jesus, claiming that what was prophesied of him was said of themselves.” We do not know, then, whether Celsus knew of any who came into the world and wished to do something like what Jesus did, and to proclaim themselves sons of God or a power of God. But since we examine these matters with a love of truth, we shall say that a certain Theudas arose among the Jews before the birth of Jesus, “saying that he was somebody great”; and when he died, those he had deceived were scattered (Acts 5:36). After him, “in the days of the census” (Acts 5:37), about the time when Jesus seems to have been born (Luke 2:1–2), a certain Judas the Galilean led many of the Jewish people to revolt with him, as a wise man and one bringing in something new. When he too paid the penalty, his teaching was overthrown, and it survived only among a very small number indeed.

After the time of Jesus, too, Dositheus the Samaritan wished to persuade the Samaritans that he was the Christ prophesied by Moses, and he seemed to have won some over by his teaching. But it is not unreasonable to quote what was said, very wisely, by Gamaliel, as recorded in the Acts of the Apostles, to show how those men were strangers to the promise, being neither sons of God nor powers of his, while Christ Jesus was truly the Son of God. Gamaliel said there: “If this plan and this word are from men, they will be overthrown,” as the movements of those men were overthrown when they died; “but if it is from God, you will not be able to overthrow this man’s teaching, or you may even be found fighting against God” (Acts 5:38–39).

Simon the Samaritan magician also wished to steal some away by his magic (Acts 8:9–11). At that time he did deceive them; but now, I think, it is not possible to find Simonians in the whole world numbering thirty in all, and perhaps I have put the number higher than it is. There are very few of them around Palestine, and in the rest of the world, through which he wished to spread his glory, his name is nowhere found. For wherever it is known, it is known from the Acts of the Apostles; it is Christians who say these things about him, and the plain facts have borne witness that Simon was nothing divine.

title: Magi, not Chaldaeans, and the new star
english: After this, Celsus’s Jew, in place of the magi in the Gospel (Matthew 2:1–2), says that Jesus has told of Chaldaeans: that they were stirred at his birth and came to worship him as God while he was still an infant, and made this known to Herod the tetrarch; and that Herod sent men to kill those born at that same time, thinking that he would destroy Jesus along with them, for fear that, if he lived long enough, he might become king (Matthew 2:16).

Notice here, then, the misunderstanding of a man who does not distinguish magi from Chaldaeans, and has not observed that their professions are different, and so has told lies about the Gospel Scripture. I do not know how it is that he has also kept silent about what moved the magi, and has not said that it was a “star” seen by them “in the East,” as it is written (Matthew 2:2). Let us see, then, what must be said in answer to this too.

We think that the “star” seen “in the East” (Matthew 2:2) was new, and not like any of the familiar ones, neither those in the sphere of the fixed stars nor those in the lower spheres; but that it was of the same kind as the comets that appear from time to time, or the beams, or the bearded stars, or the jars, or whatever names the Greeks like to give to their different kinds. We establish this point in the following way.

title: Comets and the star Balaam foretold
english: It has been observed that such stars rise at the time of great events and of the greatest changes in things on earth, signifying either changes of kingdoms, or wars, or whatever else can befall human beings that is able to shake things on earth. We have read in the treatise On Comets by Chaeremon the Stoic how comets have sometimes risen even when good things were about to happen, and he sets out the account of these cases.

If, then, the so-called comet, or some star like it, rises at the coming of new kingdoms or at other great events on earth, is it any wonder that a star should have risen at the birth of one who was going to bring something new into the human race, and to bring in a teaching not only for Jews but also for Greeks, and for many of the barbarian nations as well?

But I would say that no prophecy is on record about comets, to the effect that such and such a comet will rise in such a reign or at such times. About the star that rose at the birth of Jesus, however, Balaam prophesied, as Moses recorded, saying: “A star will rise out of Jacob, and a man will rise up out of Israel” (Numbers 24:17). And if we must also examine what is recorded about the magi at the birth of Jesus, and about the appearing of the star (Matthew 2:1–12), we would say something like this, part of it to Greeks and part to Jews.

title: The magi, the demons, and the star
english: To the Greeks, then, we would say this. Magi, who have dealings with demons and summon them for the purposes they have learned and desire, achieve such things only so long as nothing more divine and more powerful than the demons and the incantation that summons them appears or is spoken. But if some more divine manifestation takes place, the workings of the demons are overthrown, since they cannot face the light of the Godhead. It is likely, then, that at the birth of Jesus too, since “a multitude of the heavenly host,” as Luke recorded and as I believe, praised God and said, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill among men” (Luke 2:13–14), the demons for this reason lost their strength and grew weak. Their sorcery was exposed and their working undone; they were overthrown not only by the angels who visited the region around the earth because of the birth of Jesus, but also by the soul of Jesus and the Godhead in him.

So the magi, wishing to do what they were used to doing, which they had formerly done by certain incantations and tricks, looked for the cause, judging that it must be a great one; and seeing a sign from God in the sky, they wanted to see what it signified. It seems to me, then, that they had the prophecies of Balaam, which Moses also recorded, since Balaam himself had been skilled in such arts. There they found what is said about the star, and the words, “I will show him, but not now; I call him blessed, but he will not draw near” (Numbers 24:17). From this they guessed that the man foretold together with the star had come into the world; and having concluded beforehand that he was stronger than all the demons and than the beings that usually appeared to them and worked for them, they wished “to worship” him (Matthew 2:2).

They came, then, to Judea, convinced that some “king” had been born (Matthew 2:2), or knowing where he would be born, but not understanding over what kind of kingdom he would reign. They brought “gifts,” and these they “offered” to one who was, if I may call him so, a kind of compound of God and mortal man: gold as a symbol for a king, myrrh as for one who would die, and frankincense as for God (Matthew 2:11). And they “offered” them after they had learned the place of his birth (Matthew 2:9–11). But since the Saviour of the human race, who exists above the angels who help human beings, was God, an angel repaid the magi for their reverence in worshipping Jesus: he warned them not to go to Herod but to return to their own country by another way (Matthew 2:12).

title: Herod’s plot and the kingdom not of this world
english: If Herod plotted against the newborn child, it is no wonder, even if Celsus's Jew does not believe that this really happened. For wickedness is a blind thing, and wants to defeat what is destined, as though it were stronger. This is what happened to Herod too. He believed that a king of the Jews had been born, and yet he held a conviction at odds with that belief, not seeing that either the child was certainly a king and would reign, or he would not reign and to kill him would be pointless. So he wanted to kill him, his judgements set at war with one another by his wickedness, moved by the blind and wicked devil, who from the beginning plotted against the Saviour, imagining him to be someone great and to be destined for greatness.

An “angel,” then, preserving the order of events, warned Joseph, even if Celsus does not believe it, to withdraw with the child and his mother “into Egypt” (Matthew 2:13); and Herod “killed” all the children “in Bethlehem” and “in its region” (Matthew 2:16), thinking to kill along with them the king of the Jews who had been born. For he did not see the sleepless power that guards those who are worthy to be guarded and kept safe for the salvation of human beings. Of these the first of all, greater in honour and in every kind of excellence, was Jesus. He was to be a king, not as Herod supposed, but as it befitted God to give a kingdom, for the good of those who are ruled, to one who would do his subjects no middling or indifferent good, if I may so call it, but would train them and bring them under laws that are truly God's. Jesus knew this; and while he denied that he was a king in the sense in which most people understand it, he taught what sets his own kingdom apart when he said: “If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would be fighting, so that I would not be handed over to the Jews; but as it is, my kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36).

If Celsus had seen this, he would not have said: “If it was so that you might not grow up and reign in his place, why, now that you have grown up, do you not reign? Why do you, the Son of God, go about begging so ignobly, cowering for fear and wandering wretchedly up and down?”

But it is not ignoble to steer around dangers with deliberate purpose and not rush straight into them, not out of fear of death but so that, by his useful stay in this life, he might help others, until the fitting time should come for the one who had taken on human nature to die a human death, a death that brought something of use to human beings. This is plain to anyone who has understood that Jesus died for human beings; and of this we have spoken, as well as we could, in what came before.

title: Unlettered apostles and the power of their preaching
english: After this, since Celsus, not even knowing the number of the apostles, said that Jesus “attached to himself ten or eleven notorious men, tax collectors and sailors of the worst sort, and with them ran away here and there, gathering his food in a shameful and beggarly way,” come, let us deal with these points too, as far as we can. It is plain to those who read the Gospel accounts, which Celsus seems not even to have read, that Jesus chose twelve apostles (Matthew 10:1–4), of whom Matthew was a tax collector (Matthew 10:3). By those whom he loosely called sailors he perhaps means James and John, since they left the boat and “their father Zebedee” and followed Jesus (Matthew 4:21–22). For Peter and his brother Andrew, who used a casting net to get the food they needed, must be counted not among sailors but, as Scripture recorded, among fishermen (Matthew 4:18). Granted that Levi too, a tax collector, followed Jesus (Mark 2:14); yet he was not of the number of his apostles, except in some copies of the Gospel according to Mark. Of the rest we have not learned the trades by which they earned their food before they became disciples of Jesus.

To this, then, I say that those who are able to examine the story of the apostles of Jesus with good sense and fairness can see that these men taught Christianity by divine power and succeeded in winning people over to the word of God. For what was in them and won over their hearers was not a power of speech or an ordered delivery shaped by the dialectical or rhetorical arts of the Greeks. It seems to me that if Jesus had chosen men who were wise in the opinion of the multitude and able to think and speak in a way that pleases crowds, and had used them as ministers of his teaching, he would with very good reason have been suspected of having been proclaimed by a method like that of philosophers who stand at the head of some school. Then the claim that the message is divine would no longer have shone out, since the message and the preaching would have rested on the persuasiveness of a wisdom that lies in the phrasing and arrangement of words (1 Corinthians 2:4); and “faith,” like the faith that the philosophers of the world have in their doctrines, would have been “in the wisdom of men” and not “in the power of God” (1 Corinthians 2:5).

But as it is, the Gospel records that these fishermen and tax collectors had not learned even their first letters (Acts 4:13), and on this point Celsus has believed them, as telling the truth about their lack of learning. Who, then, seeing such men speaking boldly not only to Jews about faith in Jesus but also preaching him among the other nations, and succeeding, would not ask where their power to persuade came from? For it was not the kind that most people are used to. And who would not say that Jesus fulfilled the words “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matthew 4:19) by some divine power in his apostles? Paul too sets this power before us, as we have also said above, when he says: “And my word and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that our faith might not be in the wisdom of men but in the power of God” (1 Corinthians 2:4–5). For, as was said in the prophets, who announced beforehand the preaching of the gospel, “The Lord gave a word to those who preach the good news with great power, the King of the powers of the beloved” (Psalm 68:11–12), so that the prophecy which says, “His word will run swiftly” (Psalm 147:15), might also be fulfilled. And indeed we see that the “sound” of the apostles of Jesus “has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 19:4; Romans 10:18).

That is why those who hear the word proclaimed with power are filled with power, and they show it in their disposition, in their life, and in their struggle for the truth even to death. But some are empty, even though they profess to believe in God through Jesus: those who seem to be brought to the word of God without having divine power. Though I have already mentioned above a saying in the Gospel spoken by the Saviour, I will nonetheless use it again now, since the moment calls for it, to show both our Saviour's foreknowledge about the preaching of the gospel, made known in a most divine way, and the strength of the word, which without teachers prevails over those who believe, by a persuasion joined with divine power. Jesus says: “The harvest is plentiful, but the labourers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers into his harvest” (Matthew 9:37–38).

title: Sinners chosen to show the healing of souls
english: Since Celsus also called the apostles of Jesus notorious men, saying that they were “tax collectors and sailors of the worst sort,” we will say about this too that he seems to believe what is written where he wishes, so that he can bring a charge against our teaching, but to disbelieve the Gospels so that he need not accept the Godhead plainly proclaimed in those same books. Yet he ought to have recognised the writers' love of truth from their record of the less creditable things, and so to have believed them about the more divine things too.

Now it is written in the catholic epistle of Barnabas, from which Celsus perhaps took his claim that the apostles were notorious and of the worst sort, that Jesus “chose his own apostles, who were more lawless than all lawlessness” (Epistle of Barnabas 5:9). And in the Gospel according to Luke, Peter says to Jesus: “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord” (Luke 5:8). Paul too, who himself afterwards became an apostle of Jesus, says in the letter to Timothy: “The saying is trustworthy, that Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the first” (1 Timothy 1:15).

I do not know how Celsus forgot, or did not think, to say something about Paul, who after Jesus firmly founded the churches that are in Christ. For it is likely that he saw that the story of Paul would call for an answer from him: how Paul, after he had persecuted the church of God (Galatians 1:13) and fought bitterly against the believers, so far as to want to hand the disciples of Jesus over to death (Acts 22:4), later changed so greatly that “from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum” he “fully preached the gospel of Christ” (Romans 15:19), “making it his aim to preach the gospel” so as not to build “on someone else's foundation” (Romans 15:20), but to build where the gospel of God in Christ had not been preached at all.

What is out of place, then, if Jesus, wishing to show the human race how great a skill in healing souls he has, chose men who were notorious and of the worst sort, and led them on so far that they became a pattern of the purest character for those who were brought through them to the gospel of Christ?

title: Lives changed, in philosophy and in the Church
english: If we are going to reproach those who have changed with the life they led before, then it is time for us to accuse Phaedo as well, even though he became a philosopher, since, as the story goes, Socrates brought him over from a brothel to the study of philosophy. We shall also reproach philosophy with the dissolute life of Polemon, who succeeded Xenocrates, though there too we ought to welcome this in philosophy: that the reasoning of those who won them over had the power to draw men who had been held fast by such great evils away from them.

Among the Greeks there was one Phaedo, and I do not know whether a second, and one Polemon, who turned from a dissolute and utterly wicked life and took up philosophy. But with Jesus it was not only the twelve at that time; it has always been many times as many, who have become a company of the self-controlled and say of their former lives: “For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to all kinds of desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, hating one another; but when the kindness and love for humankind of God our Saviour appeared” (Titus 3:3–4), then “through the washing of rebirth and renewal of the Spirit, which he poured out on us richly” (Titus 3:5–6), we became what we are. For God “sent his word and healed them, and rescued them from their corruptions” (Psalm 107:20), as the one who prophesied in the Psalms taught.

To what has been said I might add this. Chrysippus, in his book on the treatment of the passions, in order to check the passions of the soul in human beings, tries to treat those held fast by the passions according to the various schools, without laying claim to know which doctrine is the true one. He says that even if pleasure is the end, the passions must be treated in this way; and even if there are three kinds of goods, those caught in the passions must, on this reasoning, be freed from them in this way none the less.

But the accusers of Christianity do not see in how many people the passions are checked, and in how many the flood of wickedness, and how many people’s savage characters are tamed, by means of the word. They, who boast of their public spirit, ought to have given it thanks for turning people away from many evils by a new method, and to have borne witness to it, if not that it is true, at least that it is of benefit to the human race.

title: Wise flight, and the women who provided
english: Jesus taught his disciples not to be rash, and said to them: “If they persecute you in this city, flee to the other; and if they persecute you in the other, flee again to another” (Matthew 10:23). And as he taught them, he became for them an example of a steady life, one that takes care not to go out to meet dangers at random, or at the wrong time, or without good reason. Here again Celsus maliciously misrepresents this, and his Jew says to Jesus: “With your disciples you run away, now here, now there.”

We shall say that the story told of Aristotle is just like what he slanders in Jesus and his disciples. For Aristotle saw that a court was about to be assembled against him as an impious man, because of certain doctrines of his philosophy which the Athenians thought impious. He withdrew from Athens and held his school at Chalcis, and he explained himself to his pupils, saying: “Let us leave Athens, so that we may not give the Athenians an occasion to bring on themselves a second guilt like their guilt over Socrates, and so that they may not commit impiety against philosophy a second time.”

He also says that Jesus “went about with his disciples collecting their food in a disgraceful and beggarly way.” Let him tell us where he found the disgrace and the beggarliness in this collecting. For in the Gospels “certain women” who “had been healed of” their “infirmities,” among whom was “Susanna,” provided the disciples with food “out of their own means” (Luke 8:2–3). Which of those who practised philosophy and devoted themselves to the good of their pupils did not receive from them what they needed? Or did the philosophers do this fittingly and well, while the disciples of Jesus, when they do the same, are accused by Celsus of “collecting their food in a disgraceful and beggarly way”?

title: Why the child was taken to Egypt
english: After this, Celsus’s Jew goes on to say to Jesus: “Why did you also, while still an infant, have to be carried off to Egypt, so that you would not be slaughtered? For it was not likely that a god would be afraid of death. Yet an angel came from heaven ordering you and your family to flee, so that you would not be left behind and die (Matthew 2:13). Could the great God, who had already sent two angels on your account, not keep his own Son safe right there?”

In these words Celsus supposes that what is said of Jesus is not that there was something divine in a human body and soul, but that his body too was of the kind that the myths of Homer present. At any rate, mocking the blood of Jesus that was poured out on the cross, he says that it was not “ichor, such as flows in the blessed gods” (Homer, Iliad 5.340).

We, however, believe Jesus himself when he says of the divinity that was in him, “I am the way and the truth and the life” (John 14:6), and whatever else is like this; and when he declares of his being in a human body, “But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth” (John 8:40). So we say that he became a composite being. And it was right that he who was taking thought for his own sojourn in this life as a man should not go out at the wrong time to meet a mortal danger. So too he had to be led by those who brought him up, who were guided by a divine angel. First the angel who gave the divine message said: “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife, for what has been begotten in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1:20); and a second time: “Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and stay there until I tell you; for Herod is about to search for the child, to destroy him” (Matthew 2:13).

What is recorded in these passages does not seem to me at all extraordinary. For in both places of Scripture the angel is said to have spoken these words to Joseph in a dream (Matthew 1:20; 2:13); and to be shown in a dream to do this or that happens to many other people as well, whether it is an angel or some other being that brings images before the soul. What is absurd, then, in this: that he who had once become man should also be guided in a human way so as to avoid dangers? This was not because it was impossible for things to happen otherwise, but because what was possible had to be arranged, step by step and in due order, for the safety of Jesus.

And it was certainly better that the child Jesus should slip away from Herod’s plot and go abroad with those who were bringing him up “into Egypt” “until the death” of the one plotting against him (Matthew 2:14–15), than that the providence watching over Jesus should hinder the free choice of Herod, who wanted to kill the child; or that it should put about Jesus what the poets call the “cap of Hades” (Homer, Iliad 5.845), or something like it; or that it should strike those who came to kill him, as the men in Sodom were struck (Genesis 19:11). For help given to him in a wholly extraordinary and more conspicuous way would not have served his purpose: to teach that he, a man to whom God bore witness, had something more divine within the man who was seen. That more divine element was he who is Son of God in the proper sense, God the Word (John 1:1), the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24), the one called Christ.

But now is not the time to set out what concerns the composite being, and of what elements Jesus, who became man, was made up; for this is a question that is, if I may call it so, a family matter for believers.

title: The sons of the gods and the work of Jesus
english: After this, Celsus’s Jew, as though he were some Greek fond of learning and schooled in Greek literature, says: “The ancient myths that gave a divine descent to Perseus and Amphion and Aeacus and Minos (and even these we did not believe) still showed great and wonderful works of theirs, truly beyond human power, so that they would not seem unbelievable. But you, what fine or wonderful thing have you done, in deed or in word? You showed us nothing, although we challenged you in the temple to produce some clear sign that you were the Son of God.”

To this we must say: let the Greeks show us, from any of those listed, some work that was of use to human life, brilliant, reaching down to later generations, and so great that it lends credibility to the myth about them that says they were born of divine seed. But in the men he named they will show nothing that comes even close to what Jesus displayed; unless, that is, the Greeks lead us back to myths and to the stories told among them, wanting us to believe those without reason but to disbelieve these even after so much clear evidence.

We ourselves, then, say that the whole inhabited world of human beings holds the work of Jesus; in it dwell, as sojourners, the churches of God through Jesus, made up of those who have turned from countless evils. And still the name of Jesus drives madness from people’s minds, and demons, and diseases as well. And it produces a wonderful gentleness, composure of character, love for humankind, kindness and mildness in those who have not pretended for the sake of a livelihood or some human need, but have sincerely accepted the teaching about God and Christ and the judgment to come.

title: Jesus and the sorcerers
english: Next, Celsus, wary of the great works that will be shown to have been done by Jesus, of which we have mentioned a few out of many, pretends to grant that everything recorded is true: the healings, or the raising from the dead, or the few loaves that fed many people and left much over (Matthew 14:17–20), or whatever other marvels he thinks the disciples invented and recorded. And he adds to them: “Come, let us believe that these things were done by you.”

And at once he puts them on a level with the works of sorcerers, as though these promised still more wonderful things, and with the feats performed by those who learned from the Egyptians, who sell their solemn lore for a few obols in the middle of the market-place, drive demons out of people, blow away diseases, call up the souls of heroes, display costly dinners, tables, cakes and dishes that do not exist, and make things move as though they were alive, though they are not truly living things but only appear so to the imagination. And he says: “Since those men do these things, shall we then have to think them sons of God? Or must we say that these are the practices of wicked and wretched men?”

You see how by these words he in effect admits that magic exists. I do not know whether he is the same man who wrote several books against magic. In any case, since it serves his present purpose, he likens what is recorded of Jesus to the works of magic. And they would be alike if Jesus, like the conjurers, had gone no further than a display. But as it is, none of the sorcerers uses what he does to call those who watch to the reform of their characters, nor trains in the fear of God those who are astonished at the spectacle, nor tries to persuade those who saw it to live as people who are to be justified by God. Sorcerers do none of these things, because they cannot, or do not even wish or want to concern themselves with the amendment of human beings, being themselves full of the most shameful and infamous sins.

But he, by the wonders he worked, called those who saw what was happening to the reform of their characters; how, then, is it not likely that he offered himself, not only to his genuine disciples but to the others as well, as an example of the best life? His purpose was that the disciples should be spurred on to teach people according to the will of God, and that the others, taught more fully how one ought to live by his word, or by his character and his wonders as well, should do everything with the aim of pleasing the God who is over all. If such was the life of Jesus, how could anyone reasonably compare him with the sorcerers in their aims, and not believe, as is proclaimed of him, that he is God who appeared in a human body for the good of our race?

title: Whether a body like his could be God’s
english: After this, muddling his argument and bringing what is said by a certain sect against all who follow the divine word, as though these were charges common to Christians, he says: “A body such as yours could not belong to a god.” But to this we reply that, coming into this life from a woman, he took on a human body, one capable of human death. That is why, among other things, we say that he also became a great contender: because his human body was “tempted in all things” like all human beings, yet not, as human beings are, with sin, but wholly “without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). For it is plain to us “that he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22; Isaiah 53:9). And him who “knew no sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21) God delivered up, as one pure, for all who have sinned (Romans 8:32).

Then Celsus says: “A body begotten as you were begotten, Jesus, would not be the body of a god.” Yet he suspected that, if Jesus had been born as it is written, his body could in some way be more divine, even in the eyes of most people, and in a certain sense a body of God. But in fact he does not believe what is recorded about his conception from the Holy Spirit (Matthew 1:18, 20; Luke 1:35), and he believes that he was begotten by a certain Panthera who seduced the virgin. That is why he said: “A body begotten as you were begotten would not be the body of a god.” But we have spoken about these things at greater length above.

title: His eating and his voice
english: He says: “Nor does the body of a god eat such food,” on the ground that he can show from the Gospel writings that Jesus ate, and what kind of food he ate. Well, let it be so: let him say that Jesus ate the Passover with his disciples, not only saying, “I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you” (Luke 22:15), but also eating it; and let him say that Jesus also became thirsty and drank at Jacob's well (John 4:6–7). What has this to do with what we say about his body? And he is plainly shown to have eaten fish after the resurrection (Luke 24:42–43). For according to us he took on a body, as one “born of a woman” (Galatians 4:4).

“But neither,” he says, “does the body of a god use such a voice, or such a way of persuading.” These objections too are trivial and wholly contemptible. For it will be said to him that he whom the Greeks believe to be a god, the Pythian and Didymaean, uses a voice of just this kind, that of the Pythia or of the prophetess who served at Miletus; and yet the Greeks do not on that account charge the Pythian or the Didymaean, or any other Greek god of this kind enshrined in a single place, with not being a god. But it was far better than this for God to use a voice which, because it was proclaimed with power, produced in those who heard it a persuasion beyond words.

title: Abuse is not argument
english: Then, abusing Jesus, this man, who for his impiety and his depraved doctrines is, if I may say so, hateful to God, says: “These were the doings of a depraved sorcerer, hateful to God.” And yet, if names and things are examined strictly, it will be impossible for a human being to be hateful to God, since God loves all things that exist and abhors none of the things he has made; for he did not make anything that he hated (Wisdom of Solomon 11:24). And if some prophetic expressions say something of this kind, they will be explained by this general principle: that Scripture uses expressions about God as about one who has human feelings.

But what need is there to say anything in defence against a man who thinks that, in what he professes to be persuasive arguments, he must use slander and abuse, as though Jesus were a depraved man and a sorcerer? For this is the work not of one who demonstrates, but of one who has given way to an unschooled and unphilosophical passion, when he ought to set out the matter, examine it fairly, and say in reply to it, as far as he can, whatever occurs to him.

But since Celsus's Jew has ended his speech to Jesus here, we too shall close our first book in reply to him at about this point. And if God grants the truth that destroys false arguments, according to the prayer that says, “In your truth destroy them” (Psalm 54:5), we shall begin in what follows on the second speech that Celsus puts into a character's mouth, in which he has made his Jew say what comes next to those who have been persuaded by Jesus.
